We demonstrate the topological equivalence of all intermediate beta-transformations with a specific type of greedy beta-transformation that incorporates a hole at zero. By employing this equivalence, we obtain a detailed characterization of these transformations, yielding new insights and results in various areas, such as Krieger embeddings, survivor sets, Hausdorff dimensions, bifurcation sets, and badly approximable numbers. We show that certain classes of sets associated with these beta-transformations possess unique properties, specifically that they are winning in Schmidt games and have the countable intersection property.

Determining the CP-violating phase phi_s resulting from mixing-induced phenomena in Bs decays is a crucial method for discovering potential new physics phenomena. Utilizing approximately 7,421 +/- 105 signal events from predominantly CP-odd final states (J/\psi pi+ pi-), which were isolated in 1/fb of pp collision data gathered at a 7 TeV energy level by the LHCb detector, researchers performed a time-dependent analysis on the obtained data. As a result, phi_s was estimated to be -0.019 +/- 0.173 +/- 0.004 radians, in alignment with the Standard Model predictions. Furthermore, their findings revealed no indication of direct CP violation.

It is evident that deep neural networks excel in extracting relevant features from a given dataset, but they may not necessarily excel in adapting these features to datasets with different underlying characteristics. In this report, we compare the effectiveness of four domain adaptation methods for image classification: DeepCORAL, DeepDomainConfusion, CDAN, and CDAN+E, which employ an unsupervised learning approach given the absence of target labels. Our analysis of these methods is performed using the office-31 dataset, with a GitHub repository detailing the report available at: https://github.com/agrija9/Deep-Unsupervised-Domain-Adaptation.

In finite fields of dimension 2, an arc is a subset where no 3 points share a line. To determine the total number of such arcs, a specific count is established for small sized fields and an approximation is found for larger fields with a specific rate of accuracy.

A pictorial proof shows that there are $\binom{n+2}{4}$ equilateral triangles in a regular $n$-sided triangle by establishing a one-to-one correspondence between four-element subsets of the set $\{1, 2, \dots, n+2\}$ and the equilateral triangles in the $n$-sided triangle, where it's essential to visualize the scenario to verify the proof's validity.

Despite recent advancements in Graph Neural Networks (GNNs), explaining their predictive decisions remains an unresolved issue. Current methods primarily address the interpretation of individual cases (i.e., important graph structures and node attributes) on a post-hoc basis, but neglect the underlying reasons for a case's classification. While many inferences are classified as either positive or negative examples, we focus on binary classes for this study. We introduce a new approach, ProPS-GNN, that utilizes case characteristics to identify distinguishing features between classes, thereby explaining comparison cases and making unseen examples predictable. ProPS-GBN significantly outperformed the benchmark methods in various synthetic and real-world scenarios, achieving up to a 25% increase in Area Under ROC Curve (AUC) in our experiments.

The peculiar system, RXCJ0232.2-4420, at $z$ = 0.18, contains a unique radio halo surrounding its central cluster core. To explore its development and composition, we examined archival X-ray data from Chandra and XMM-Newton, examining its hot gas up to 2 Mpc radius. Its overall cooling time, however, cannot be determined due to the absence of energy core. Analyzing the gamma value, a value of 0.5 indicates the presence of a cool core, but other characteristics do not support this, suggesting RXCJ0232.2-4420 does not have a typical formation path for high-frequency radio emissions. Further investigation showed that radio emissions do not align with gas distribution or temperature gradients, excluding secondary magnetic fields. Merger activity, however, could be the primary driver for both halo formation and radio emissions.

Recently, the Legendre Memory Unit (LMU), a novel type of recurrent neural network, was developed and has demonstrated superior performance on various benchmark datasets. In this work, the linear component of the LMU is optimized and refined to facilitate training, leading to improved performance on real-world datasets. In comparison to the original LMU and other prominent deep learning structures such as LSTMs and transformers, the enhanced linear LMU achieves exceptional results on tasks including MNIST, CIFAR-10, and IMDB, thus showcasing its versatility and potential as a reliable replacement for traditional recurrent networks and more recent transformer models.

As the next decade unfolds, the field of particle physics is driven to answer several fundamental questions. A key area of interest is whether particles like dark matter or a new fundamental force exist. Several promising candidates are being investigated, including the $6~\mathrm{keV}$ neutralino and the $1~\mathrm{MeV}$ scalar dark matter, both of which are investigate-able with proposed facilities. In this paper, an extensive review of feebly interacting particles, including dark matter and neutrino-related topics, is presented with a focus on experimental research. A key aspect of the paper is an in-depth discussion of dark matter detection with ly$\beta$-decaying dark matter, the Dark Matter Reload, and X-ray filters with a focus on current experimental research. In addition, Dark Matter Spinning Top and sub-Torr load-in devices are two newly proposed experimental research facilities that are presented in detail. These facilities are part of an extensive research program aimed at exploring new facilities to investigate new physics. A key aspect of the program is partnering with existing research facilities to speed up the investigation process. For example, partner-ship with existing research facilities such as LUX will allow for faster progress at new facilities like Dark Matter Spinning Top. Language plays a vital role in a culture's identity, shaping communities and leaving a lasting legacy, even long after a language is classified as extinct. In reality, the disappearance of a language doesn't necessarily mean a culture has vanished. In this article, research is conducted to examine how languages interact and coexist within a multilingual setting. A simple mathematical model is developed to analyze language diffusion among neighboring groups, and it's found that the migration of individuals between these groups significantly contributes to the development of isolated monolingual communities. Furthermore, the model's results are linked to the anatomical characteristics of human languages, and it's discovered that the model's parameters are in line with real-world language data. Moreover, the model predicts the likelihood of a small isolated group developing its unique language, and it's used to examine how this influences the diversity of languages within a broader population.

PINN algorithms have made significant breakthroughs in solving various complex PDE-based problems. Despite the potential of these algorithms to achieve high accuracy, their convergence often gets hindered by the problem's characteristics. In this research, we delve into the effectiveness of using wider neural network architectures to improve the convergence of PINN algorithms. Focusing on a multi-scale periodic PDE scenario, we observe that increasing the network width enables the model to more effectively capture high-frequency features in the problem. Building on this understanding, we apply the concept of 'neural network width' as a variable in the model's training process. The outcome reveals a positive correlation between the network width, input dimension, and model convergence. The relationship between the network width, training efficiency, and convergence is particularly notable at high input dimensions. Based on these findings, we recommend incorporating a variable network width model into the standard PINN training framework. The proposed method trains the network's width alongside its other parameters, along with its weights and biases, allowing it to adapt to problem-specific features. The approach shows promising results in optimizing the training process for PINN algorithms.

We examine a two-wave system in the interval (-1,1), where one wave absorbs energy and the other does not, with partial damping that mimics a material behavior called Kelvin-Voigt damping. Prior research showed that with damping throughout the entire domain, the system's energy decreases at a rate proportional to $t^{-\frac{1}{2}}$. Using the frequency domain method in this paper, we demonstrate the system's behavior changes significantly when the damping is limited and show that the decay rate can be much slower, specifically we find it to be at least $t^{-\frac{1}{20}}$.

Recent advances in deep reinforcement learning have led to widespread success across various applications, yet deep RL methods struggle with two key limitations: efficiency and transparency. High interaction costs underscore the importance of efficiency, while improved transparency via more interpretable models fosters trust from users.  Unlike prior research, our approach does not assume pre-built feature extractors but rather leverages the inherent representational power of pre-trained models. By applying clustering and regularization techniques to these representations, we effectively simplify the high-dimensional signal, yielding substantial interaction cost reductions and more transparent learning pathways for policy optimization.

We've developed a method to produce optical nonreciprocity using quantum squeezing in ring cavity configurations. By applying squeezing to one resonator, we can create a strong advantage for a specific optical mode, allowing it to overcome backflow and establish a high transmission rate in double-nonlinearity interferometers. Compared to previous schemes using nonlinear phases or techniques based on forward/backward modes, our approach achieves comparable or higher nonreciprocal transmission rates, alongside lower required nonlinearities and fewer optical components. Importantly, we can independently manage the nonreciprocal properties of individual resonator modes, making it possible to achieve asymmetric modes within a single-nonlinearity system. Furthermore, we can utilize quantum squeezing of a weak light source to achieve significant optical nonrecality, without requiring excessive power from a pump source. Additionally, we've identified that quantum squeezing of ringing modes can provide robustness against pump field misalignment, minimizing the need for precise alignment and, consequently, reducing potential losses.

We expand upon the research initiated by P. D. Jonathan and A. M. Jonathan in their 2021 paper by examining a function f, defined as the sum of a series of concave kernel functions, in the open interval from 0 to 1, including all these intervals. The functions are then differentiated and represented as a sum of alternating power series. This enables identification of their representations, relationships, and a key lemma concerning their behavior, particularly focusing on a function defined as $\arctan$ in the given interval. The functions behave symmetrically and have a significant connection to the $\arctan$ function.

The CRESST experiment is one of the most sensitive experiments in exploring the direct detection of dark matter, particularly effective for detecting light mass particles through the use of $^{136}$Xe nuclear reactions when operating at the LNGS underground research facility. To further improve its prospects for discovering new physics beyond the standard model, the $^{116}$Cd enrichment of the experiment's target crystals has been implemented. These enriched crystals contain a high concentration of the isotopic variant of cadmium that offers exceptional sensitivity to specific particles hypothesized in models of beyond-standard model physics. Additionally, the experiment's ability to investigate multiple physics processes in various energy ranges will allow for more in-depth analysis. The current development of enriched crystals, destined for the CRESST SIANA experiment, are detailed in this report.

Blind Image deblurring attempts to estimate a latent image's sharpness and a blurred image, which is often ambiguous and has multiple solutions. The uncertainty can be represented by a mixture of Gaussian functions, where each component captures a specific mode. The traditional approach for defining the Gaussian components relies on random initial guesses, which may lead to either underfit or overfit. To address these issues, a proposed method called KBlind involves a two-step process. Firstly, it determines a set of meaningful kernel bases as initial candidates for the Gaussian mixtures. Secondly, it iteratively refines the weight of each kernel by evaluating the data's residual. The method is evaluated using several blind deblurring datasets and is found to be effective in representing the image deblurring residual's complexity with a low number of kernels.

This paper introduces a new concept called associative BiHom-Yang-Baxter pair with weight (λ,γ) which can be used to solve the double curved Rota-Baxter system. Furthermore, we establish equivalent definitions of covariant Rota-Baxter operators in Hom-lean algebroids and show their relationship with associative BiHom-Yang-Baxter pairs. A generalized version of the Hom-lean algebroid, known as pseudo-assocative Hom-lean algebroid, is also defined. Lastly, we outline the characteristics of double curved Rota-Baxter systems in a specific type of Hom-lean algebra.

Formal verification offers critical correctness assurances for software,
particularly vital in systems requiring safety and security assurances.
Hoare logic serves as a widely employed formal methodology for systematically
verifying software adherence to specifications. Although, the application of
formal methodologies relies heavily on being able to express a specification in a
formidable formal logic. Yet, the formal language employed for specifying program
requirements frequently hinders understanding of the software design and operational
behavior. A novel approach to specifying and evaluating software requirements utilizes
a descriptive formal logic called FOL* that facilitates the integration of a program's
designed schema and operational functionalities. In this paper, the semantic basis
of FOL* is characterized through the utilization of higher-order functions, providing a
clearly defined and operative schema for assessing program satisfaction relative to a
particular specification within FOL*. As evidence of its utility and applicability, the
paper presents instances of software verifications conducted using FOL*. Furthermore,
the work illustrates instances of software design artifacts that can be employed for
verifying and evaluating programs.

Distributed consensus is crucial for various distributed systems, such as distributed databases and blockchains. The Canopus protocol efficiently manages fast, large-scale distributed consensus without costly virtualization. The canopus protocol achieves Canopus consensus through fast mixing of hash values and a virtualized, fault-tolerant mechanism called Fault++ that compensates for fault recovery shortfalls of underlying fault tolerance methods. The Canopus protocol demonstrates robust performance even under extreme stress and high throughput even when stress is applied. The statistical canopus protocol offers improved fault tolerance and faster recovery at a cost to performance.

Recent studies utilizing neutron spin echo and nuclear magnetic resonance relaxation methods, which examine linear transport properties, have yielded contrasting results when interpreting the impact of cholesterol on the bending modulus of lipid bilayers. This inconsistency arose despite earlier research employing solely equilibrium experiments, not linear transport properties, indicating that one may be misled by data from the latter. A general discussion highlights how this misunderstanding occurs, after which it's demonstrated that the neutron spin echo findings can be reinterpreted to be consistent with the prior equilibrium results, specifically those involving cholesterol's effect on the bending modulus of lipid bilayers. Furthermore, it's shown that a threshold threshold exists below which cholesterol's effect on the membrane's bending modulus becomes undetectable.

This paper examines the loop quantum cosmological model generated from the ADM Hamiltonian. It looks at a spatially homogeneous, flat FRW model and finds that its modified Friedmann equation is analogous to that of the APS LQC model. Notably, the model's critical matter density at the bounce point is a quarter of the original APS LQC model, with the critical density $\rho_{cL}$ equalling $\frac{\rho_{c}}{4}$. This discovery implies that quantum gravity effects will manifest earlier than previously thought and also make detection potentially easier.

The Pierre Auger Observatory catalog details 100 extensive air-showers 
recorded between 2004 and 2020 for high-energy particles, spanning a specific
energy range from 78 to 166 EeV. This comprehensive dataset is made available 
for close examination, alongside nine events used to establish the energy scale 
for each detected primary particle. An accompanying plot displays the locations 
where these energetic particles entered Earth's atmosphere, leaving their data unanalyzed.

Incorporating deep neural networks into robotic systems poses a significant problem due to the lack of reliable measures for their output predictions. Researchers have developed uncertainty estimation methods for deep object detectors but encountered difficulties with information loss during non-maximum suppression and the multitasking nature of anchor-based object detection. Our novel solution, Dubin-Influence Variance (DIVar), overcomes these limitations by introducing a novel uncertainty quantification technique for deep neural networks. DIVar employs a differentiable approach using a mathematical Dubin filter to smoothly propagate uncertainty from object detection to non-maximum suppression, resulting in a reliable and efficient method for quantifying model uncertainty in deep object detectors. Experimental evaluations on the MS-COCO dataset demonstrate the effectiveness and practicality of DIVar, highlighting its potential as an innovative approach for uncertainty quantification in object detection.

The integration of advanced traffic forecasting technology significantly benefits traffic management, traffic counting, and associated monetary expenses. However, predicting future traffic states using real-world data collected by video cameras is complicated by the presence of missing data, where roads are obstructed by trees, buildings, and other obstacles. To address this issue, we propose a novel spatio-temporal forecasting approach that breaks down test data into smaller patches to accommodate diverse sizes of missing data gaps. Similar to existing techniques, our method also incorporates correlations both in time and space as well as past predictions to produce high-quality predictions. By testing our proposed approach on two public datasets, we demonstrate that it effectively handles sequences with and without missing data, yielding comparable results to state-of-the-art models in terms of prediction accuracy. Notably, our approach surpasses current models in handling cases with extensive missing data, showcasing its robustness and practical utility.

In recent years, rewriting frameworks have been established for various n-categories, enabling the efficient manipulation and computation within these systems. Motivated by the connection between Gray categories and tricategories, we developed a dual transformation framework for Gray categories, which we demonstrate to be equivalent to the tricategory structure.

Automatic hippocampus segmentation on magnetic resonance imaging is a critical component in the diagnosis and research of neuropsychiatric disorders. Current deep learning-based techniques require extensive datasets for training and may not adequately account for individual differences in hippocampus structure. However, these methods fall short when applied to diverse populations, including older adults, patients with hippocampal damage, or those on medication. In response to these limitations, this research introduces HipSegNET, a new convolutional neural network designed to segment the hippocampus from T1-weighted MR images without extensive training data. In evaluation studies, HipSegNET demonstrated high performance using a small, artificially generated dataset and produced superior results compared to state-of-the-art methods on two public datasets. Additionally, HipSegNET showed expected performance on an older adult dataset that was not used for training its underlying network.

We scrutinize an experiment claiming to showcase the quantum pigeonhole effect by having three parties navigate a two-path interferometer with no pair of them using the same path simultaneously. Through an analysis based on weakly entangled initial states, we uncover inconsistencies in the claim. Our analysis also underscores the importance of accurately characterizing initial quantum states.

Our research identifies the Cosmic Ray Albedo Neutron Decay (CRAND) as the primary factor responsible for the formation of high-energy inner proton radiation belts in the South Atlantic Anomaly (SAA). Through a simulated demonstration, we show that these protons are generated by neutron interaction with the Earth's atmosphere, created as a byproduct of the High-Energy Particle (HEP) decay. Utilizing a TRAC 2D atmospheric transport model, we traced the displacement of these protons within the South Atlantic Anomaly region, revealing a unique distribution of energy and angular dispersion that diverges from normally observed proton radiation belt structures. Unlike typical proton radiation belts, which typically exhibit a distinct peak energy displacement, the protons in the SAA region consistently embody the energy embodied within the originating neutron, thereby displacing angular dispersion in favor of location dependence. This phenomenon is exemplified through a proposed explanation of the proton radiation belt's location in the SAA, where we theorize a unique equilibrium is achieved at the boundary between the South Atlantic Anomaly and the Van Allen Cup, where an equilibrium is achieved at the 230 km boundary.

Deep Neural Networks' (DNN) performance has reached a threshold, making it challenging to improve performance by increasing size.  To overcome this, researchers have focused on enhancing expressivity, the ability of a model to learn from training data.  Despite its name, expressivity is not directly related to the model's ability to represent its parameters.  In fact, a clear definition of expressivity as a model capacity characteristic is still lacking.  Our study aims to clarify expressivity by relating it to the concept of learnability and providing a formal definition.  Our findings demonstrate that expressivity is constrained by a model's ability to generalize and that certain factorization patterns restrict a model's ability to learn.  Our research also identifies promising avenues for further investigation.

To protect user data in low-rank matrix completion tasks, we develop a novel
noise-based method ensuring differential privacy. This method incorporates
noise with characteristics inspired by the Huber loss function in robust
statistics, and is termed as the Huber mechanism. In our study, we evaluate the
performance of this Huber mechanism against other privacy mechanisms, including
using the Alternating Least Squares method to solve matrix completion tasks.
Furthermore, we apply the Advanced Linear Mixing Model from machine learning to
investigate how different data generation processes impact the Huber mechanism's
privacy effectiveness. Experimental findings reveal that the Huber mechanism, as
well as a modified version that incorporates ex-post efficiency adjustments,
maintain superior privacy properties and produce highly accurate matrix
estimates.

We propose a novel approach to modelling interstellar dust where larger grains are comprised of a uniform material, referred to as 'astrodust', and tiny particles, known as PAHs, come in various distinct forms. The evidence suggests that a uniform grain composition is most consistent with the observed patterns of infrared polarization, and the established ratio between optical and infrared polarization. A detailed analysis reveals that a combination of astrodust and PAHs accurately replicates the properties of galactic extinction and emission from interstellar dust while adhering to existing constraints on dust abundance. The associated data and software have been made publicly accessible for further research.

Research on exoplanets has historically focused on more massive stars, yet recent discoveries indicate that low-mass stars too can host planets. Since it's challenging for such stars to lose their original disk material, any planets found in these systems likely formed early in their lifetime. To examine the minimum mass boundary for planetary emergence, I've carried out Monte-Carlo simulations of planetary formation using the Two-Population Three-component model. This model separates planets from dust grains and other material, with the latter decaying into the star or being ejected. Simulations assume various disk material sizes, planet formation timescales, and outcomes - either planets or runaway grains - as input. As a control, I've run the simulations for typical solar-mass stars, then adjusted key parameters for very low-mass stars, providing a benchmark for comparing planetary potential in these systems. Results show that, for random input settings, most low-mass star simulations yield negative planetary masses or no planets at all. Simulating 100 low-mass star runs yielded 13 successful planetary formations, ranging from 2 to 70 Earth-masses on average. In contrast, 100 solar-mass star simulations yielded 98 planetary formations, with masses spanning 10 to 25 Earth-masses on average. These basic model findings suggest that planetary formation in very low-mass stars is likely to be rare, but not ruled out entirely.

Consider the rules of a popular light-switching game played on a simple graph with vertices of clickable lights. Each click affects the state of the chosen light and its neighboring lights. A sequence of strategic clicks leads to winning, which means turning off all lights in a predetermined arrangement. Inspired by the original Lights Out game from Tiger Electronics, we're investigating an extension known as the Most Clicks Problem, which revolves around determining the most clicks required to solve any given configuration of lights in a grid-based graph. Given our analysis on grids of size (3k-1) by (3k-1) with Scherphius' algorithm as our benchmark, we've set our solution strategy by first reducing the problem into a weighted flow problem and then utilizing an efficient algorithm to solve for the maximum flow. A step-by-step guide to our approach is outlined, and our claimed optimal turn sequence is derived through our method. Additionally, we've also found a general formula for calculating the maximum number of clicks in an (n) by (n) grid, which we've further demonstrated with a few example cases.

This paper presents a novel, multi-stage image segmentation model, combining the capabilities of image restoration and image segmentation. The integration of image restoration techniques addresses issues of missing or distorted data, such as data loss or noisy inputs, which frequently hinder image segmentation tasks. The proposed model addresses two interconnected challenges: image restoration and segmentation, with the former addressed through initial stages and the latter through final stages. The model's design allows for flexible reconfiguration, encompassing traditional image segmentation schemes as specialized instances. Notable instances of the model include multi-stage LSSC for segmenting restored images, and the combination of LSSC and MedLSSC for challenging image segmentation tasks. Comprehensive evaluations on diverse datasets showcase the model's capabilities for restored image segmentation, including synthetic, real-world images from diverse datasets and the state-of-the-art performance on multiple benchmarks.

The first phase of abstract interpretation, known as the "upward" phase, involves a step called abstract fixpoint computation. This phase can be broken down into two stages: the "upward" and "downward" stages. The initial "upward" stage represents the initial approximation of the least post-fixpoint solution to the program's operator, followed by a "downward" stage where the result is approximated to its least pre-fixpoint solution. The combined process represents the least fixpoint solution to the program operator. The second iteration of the upward phase begins with the least fixpoint solution from the previous iteration. The downward phase followed by the upward phase constitutes the sequential process of the fixpoint computation in the first iteration. The paper focuses on the second phase of the fixpoint computation, specifically the downward phase where the iterated upward result is approximated to its least pre-fixpoint solution. The paper defines abstract fixpoint computation as a mathematical process and expresses the downward phase using continuous operators. The paper emphasizes that the fixpoint computation can be expressed using the upward phase alone; however, the application of the downward phase followed by the upward phase results in a shorter sequence compared to applying only the upward phase twice.

A broad range of structural phases in perovskite oxides host various topological phonons, which can be triggered by changes in temperature or pressure. Our study focuses on the phonon topological phase transitions in binary and ternary perovskite oxides, with particular emphasis on $t$-R3m and $a$-Fm-3m phases. Our results, based on computational simulations utilizing density functional theory and phonon density of states, show that MnO3 and CrO3 exhibit topological phonons through the formation of square and octahedral structures, which lead to phonon helical patterns in their crystal structures. Additionally, our study of YScO3, YFeO3, and GdFeO3 reveals that these compounds may also host topological phonons, which could be triggered by external stimuli. Our findings suggest the exciting potential for perovskite oxides to be integrated into new thermomechanical devices that utilize topological phonons.

Unsupervised outlier detection in various fields such as data mining and machine learning relies heavily on distance-based methods due to their adaptability in generic metric spaces. Building on an enhanced version of the edited nearest neighbors band depth, our research introduces a robust and computationally efficient outlier detection framework. The introduced depth functions capitalize on the benefits of existing depth-based methods while mitigating their drawbacks, ultimately yielding a versatile and scalable outlier detection framework. A comprehensive evaluation is conducted to validate the proposed approach using synthetic and real-world datasets across distinct metric spaces, showcasing its effectiveness.

The probability of (de-)excitation and photon emission is evaluated for a non-relativistic, moving atom interacting with a quantum electromagnetic field near a stationary, perfectly conducting plane. These findings expand upon previous scalar model outcomes where the atom was represented by a scalar variable coupled to a scalar field. This assessment considers all influences on the atom's behavior, including an adjustment to the atom's energy due to the influence of the electromagnetic field, which outlines an unbounded set of energy states for this system.

As applications relying on graph representations grow, the focus has shifted from global fairness to incorporating fairness at the node level, considering that Graph Neural Network (GNN)-based models primarily operate within local neighborhoods. To address this limitation, we propose a framework that captures the concept of neighborhood fairness. Our method is built on two core components - the first enables the construction of equitable neighborhoods for any node in a graph and the second allows adaptation to accommodate specific data constraints. Notably, while numerous studies have explored link prediction, we delve into fair link classification as part of the graph representation learning task. Through comprehensive evaluations, we showcase the effectiveness of our neighborhood fairness framework across multiple graph machine learning tasks and observe improved accuracy alongside enhanced fairness metrics.

This research focuses on kinetic models for reversible enzyme reactions and evaluates the effectiveness of two analytical techniques in obtaining approximate solutions to these models. We apply and compare the Homotopy Perturbation Method and the Simple Iteration Method to derive approximate analytical solutions to non-linear equations describing reversible enzyme reactions.  The resulting approximations demonstrate a comparable level of accuracy.  Supporting Matlab codes for both methods are provided in the appendices.

Theoretical physicists conduct experiments in final stages with data obtained from proton-proton collisions, utilizing the CMS detector at CERN. In a 2016 study with 35.9 inverse femtobarns of recorded data and 13 TeV of centre-of-mass energy, researchers searched for evidence of supersymmetry in final stages characterized by the presence of one or more jets and unobserved momentum across a line influenced by top-quark pairs. After further analysis, researchers examined models where supersymmetry no longer acts upon the top-quark sector to determine the minimum mass difference between the top-quark and its corresponding supersymmetric counterpart. In this study, researchers explored the range of possible masses for the gluino where virtual states of supersymmetric top-quark squarks may occur. Given the absence of supersymmetry during the study, researchers established upper limits for the mass of the gluino, ranging between 1670 and 1780 GeV under different scenarios. Researchers also explored the range of possible masses for the top squark and determined the minimum mass difference between the top-quark and its corresponding supersymmetric counterpart, ranging between 440 and 600 GeV. Researchers explored the range of possible masses for the Higgs boson, determined the branching ratio of specific decay processes and established the range of possible masses for the tau neutrino. Researchers explored the range of possible masses for the W boson. Researchers also explored the study's sensitivity towards discovering or excluding new physics during

Two proposed expectation models for temporary financial bubbles, involving individuals with varied predictions and positive influences, show that bubble collapse can be marked by an explosive growth in prices that suddenly ends at a potential critical point. The varied predictions among rational individuals make it difficult to synchronize their actions, causing the bubble to survive nearly up to its expected endpoint. Exact solutions from the models yield mathematical transformations enabling new tests for detecting bubbles in financial trends, thus providing tools for identifying bubble onset and forecasting termination times without the complex task of parameter estimation in stochastic equations. The effectiveness of this approach was demonstrated in testing three markets - US S&P500 from 1980-2008, US NASDAQ from 1980-2008, and Hong Kong's Hang Seng index from 1986-2008.

Quantum harmonic oscillators were computationally analyzed in their ground state with either steady-state driving forces varying in intensity or driving forces that changed over time. Calculations of position expectations were carried out for multiple scenarios of mass, angular frequency, and the lambda parameter in both cases. Constant driving led to coherent states, with theoretical predictions closely matched by both simulation approaches. A discrete-time lattice Metropolis algorithm was used to evaluate the imaginary time path integral for these simulations.

Recent research has shown significant progress in improving recommender system performance through leveraging reviews for predicting ratings, however the current methods have several limitations. The existing techniques often use complex neural networks which are difficult to understand, making it hard to integrate reviews into a scalable recommender system. Additionally, the models are not utilizing reviews which contain rich sentiment information to provide accurate predictions. We present a new approach called Sentiment-aware Recommendation Ranking (SRR), which addresses these issues by introducing a lightweight network that effectively captures review sentiment for accurate rating predictions. The proposed method learns review sentiment explicitly using a sentiment analysis model and uses two learned components, review sentiment and sentiment consistency, which are both incorporated into a hybrid model using a gradient boosting machine. Experiment results on several real-world datasets have shown the proposed method's superiority in rating predictions compared to existing models on several evaluation metrics.

Developing CS NLP systems is obstructed by the scarcity of CS data. This study delves into utilizing data augmentation methods to create Dialectal Arabic-English CS text, by replacing words with alternative choices in parallel corpora, selecting points to replace either randomly or according to word similarity, and utilizing alignment techniques to determine which words to replace. The study examines the effectiveness of using sentence splitting and merging with results showing that using basic n-gram models yields better outcomes than advanced models like Transformer, and that a hybrid approach of random and similar replacement, along with filtering, outperforms other combinations of techniques. The largest datasets generated in this study consist of 1.67M sentences (approximately 90K unique sentences) after filtering. The new data was used to retrain AR-EN neural machine translation models, resulting in improved performance on the AR-EN language model, the AR-EN translation task, and the AR-EN paraphrasing task. The study's data and code have been made publicly available.

We show that any subgroup of homeomorphisms of a compact surface that fix the boundary, whose action within the surface's interior is highly transitive, cannot be topologically compact when using the compact-open topology's inherited structure.

We're investigating integrable boundary conditions that can be geometrically interpreted as D-branes within specific theoretical models based on products of group and coset spaces, which are generalized versions of lambda deformations. Utilizing a sigma-model approach, we're examining the relevant brane geometries associated with H2, sigma-models, and Virasoro/conformal field theory (CFT) boundary conditions, and we're repurposing some of these geometries as branes in string theory. Key examples of the brane geometries we're considering include those associated with Gp, FQMs, and Virasoro field theories.

As tasks increasingly rely on computer execution, the demand for reliable solutions is rising across domains, including numerical computations and learning-based approaches. When developing or applying such methods, a properly structured mesh with the right number of accurate nodes is crucial. In the context of hexahedral elements, these meshes take the form of hexahedrons, which are now widely employed due to their suitability for complex simulations. A versatile mesh composed of these units can efficiently represent a wide range of shapes. In this research, we outline the hexahedron classification process used in the MeshClassify dataset. By combining the features of both 2D meshes and 3D hexahedrons, this dataset achieves greater diversity and comprehensiveness in class labels, enabling more effective and reliable classifications of meshes and hexahedrons. Current hexahedron classification methods face significant challenges in large-scale problems. By developing a robust classification tool based on the MeshClassify dataset and comparing the performance of various approaches, we demonstrate the potential for substantial improvements in classification efficiency, particularly in local and global scenarios.

The tasks of relation extraction and knowledge graph link prediction share a
common link in their objectives, allowing them to complement each other in the
process of predicting a subject-object relationship in a sentence. Specifically,
our approach enhances relation extraction by providing the extracted relationships
with context in a knowledge graph, whereas KGLP is enhanced through relation
extraction by verifying if the relationships predicted in a knowledge graph are
also present in training data. When both tasks are combined, our method yields
substantial improvements in performance, indicating a synergistic effect.

This study introduces an innovative analytical delay model specifically tailored for deep submicron CMOS inverters. Developed based on the critical recognition that inverter delay is a complex interplay of multiple process variables and load capacitance, the proposed model incorporates parameterized equations derived using Curve Fitting Toolbox in Matlab to accurately capture these dynamics. In comparison to simulation results generated by SPICE and the BSIM4 transistor model, the analytical delay model exhibits remarkably high precision, demonstrating an average error of less than 2% across an extensive range of technological parameters and output loads. As a result, the proposed model presents itself as a computationally efficient solution for diverse technology nodes and probabilistic gate delay characterisation applications.

Making optimal decisions in complex, continuously changing environments requires
assuming certain conditions. Often, researchers assume a certain level of consistency
in the decision-making model known as the Q-function. However, in numerous real-world scenarios,
this condition does not hold true. Instead, we propose a more adaptable way of measuring the consistency of Q-functions
in various types of task environments. This new approach enables us to establish a fundamental principle for optimal decision-making,
as well as develop methods to quantify the accuracy of decision-making in various types of task environments.

The underlying mechanisms of the ventral temporal cortex's animacy organization remain contentious, suggesting that animacy exists along a spectrum rather than a binary divide. Recent evidence suggests this continuum is influenced by the degree of presence or absence of animacy characteristics or by how entities are perceived as being social or non-social. A groundbreaking study published in Neuropsychologia in 2021 provided insight into the underlying mechanisms of the ventral temporal cortex's animacy organization by examining cases of Superior Temporal Gyrus (STG) lesions. The STG plays a pivotal role in understanding speech and social cues, including recognizing core words and facial expressions. A patient, identified as K.K., had undergone an STG/planum temporale resection and was tested using the Living Things test, a widely recognized scale that measures how individuals respond to living things, including animals and humans. Contrary to expectations, the patient showed an exceptional capacity to recognize core words and facial expressions. Furthermore, the patient demonstrated an impaired response to abstract animacy characteristics but showed a notably intact living/non-living distinction. The patient's responses were cross-correlated with neuroimput from 10 otherwise comparable patients who had undergone similar operations. A novel explanation for the underlying mechanisms of the ventral temporal cortex's animacy organization emerged. Specifically, the data support the "social continuum hypothesis," which posits that the ventral temporal cortex's animacy organization exists along a social continuum. In scientific simulation, achieving accurate replication of real-world scenarios is a top priority. However, commonly used methods such as the finite element method and finite volume method are often prone to inaccuracies and artifacts, like Gibbs oscillations, especially when approximating complex characteristics. This necessitates an efficient and accurate approach that can effectively address inconsistencies like negative concentration values or concentration exceeding 100 percent. Our proposed method employs a convex optimization technique, utilizing a convex combination of mean values from different subdomains, effectively deriving a summable and piecewise smooth convex splines solution from an oscillatory function. By building upon existing convex splines technology, we demonstrate the method's ability to address inaccuracies in problem-specific parameters like jump values, and incorporate additional constraints into the optimization process. This framework is compatible with a range of optimization problems, and we've tailored it to address hyperspectral unmixing, approximating multiple signal components within a mixture image. Our experimental results, derived from both one- and multi-dimensional test cases, demonstrate the method's ability to significantly reduce errors like oscillations, and showcase its effectiveness in addressing problem-specific inaccuracies through convex optimization.

Quasi-periodic oscillations type C, typically observed in low-hard and hard-intermediate states of black hole X-ray transients, have been investigated using the MAXI J1535-571 data collected by Insight-HXMT. By applying a novel time-dependent Comptonization model and a relativistic reflection model, researchers have demonstrated its ability to accurately describe X-ray data up to 100 keV in the hard-intermediate state. Observations show the type C QPO frequency varied between 2.1 to 3.3 Hz, and then sharply increased to ~9 Hz. This phenomenon is associated with the evolution of corona size and feedback fraction. When correlated with radio data using the correlation coefficient, it was discovered that radio emission and type C QPO showed a temporal relationship, and radio emission emerged prior to the QPO increase. This suggests that the corona reshapes and becomes more uniform to produce the QPO. During this process, it appears that the corona grazes the outer pole, causing the radio emission to enhance.

In the context of multi-agent reinforcement learning, particularly for tasks requiring cooperation and communication, MARL agents are prone to being brittle due to their potential for overfitting on the policies of their training partners. As a result, they may adapt strategies centered on preconceived expectations of other agents' actions rather than truly reacting to their behaviors. To address this issue, we developed transfer empowerment as a method that quantifies the influence between the actions of individual agents and aims to guide MARL agents toward developing reactive approaches. Three simulated cooperation scenarios confirm our hypothesis that this approach leads to improved performance in multi-agent settings, making transfer empowerment a promising principle for enhancing the effectiveness of MARL coordination through increased reactivity to partner behaviors.

We introduce MatSim, a comprehensive synthetic dataset suited for visual material recognition in everyday contexts. MatSim encompasses 38 material categories with 320 unique textures, featuring one entire roll of fabric per class, enabling diverse ocurrences and transformations. Our benchmark supports four key tasks: material classification, segmentation, segmentation-with-mask, and material transfer. To showcase the potential of visual material recognition, we establish two state adversaries - one utilizing pre-trained vision transformers and the other transfer learning from RGB-RG color spaces. Both adversaries are trained on MatSim, and we provide thorough evaluations, alongside ablation studies, to substantiate our findings. With 16,000 images and 2,400 test instances, MatSim serves as an invaluable resource for researchers and developers, spurring advancements in related areas. Furthermore, we provide source code and plan to release new datasets focused on visual material recognition.

Two equivalent formulations of Lie 2-algebras are recalled: one as a categorification of Lie algebras and another as 2-term L∞-algebras. The paper proceeds by introducing Lie 2-algebras of specific types: 2-step, 3-step, and those derived from 2-groups. These are characterized by mapping spaces in relation to their corresponding 2-group extensions. The focus then shifts to cocycles defining cohomology for these Lie 2-algebras, specifically 2-cochains. The paper concludes with an examination of the cohomology categorification of the 2-group extension of a 2-step Lie 2-algebra.

We introduce a novel method for local image feature matching, where instead of a sequential process, we first identify pixel-wise dense matches at a basic level and refine the good matches at a detailed level using a Transformer model. The challenges of using Transformers in real-time image processing are overcome by optimizing the detailed matching level to prevent unnecessary computation on low-texture areas, where feature matches are usually sparse. Additionally, we leverage the Transformer's attention mechanism to dynamically allocate computing resources. Experimental results demonstrate the benefits of our approach, particularly in low-texture scenarios, and showcase performance on the KITTI dataset that surpasses leading methods.

The paper addresses the problem of bias in vector magnetic field maps, particularly in estimating the component perpendicular to the line-of-sight, Bperp. This issue has been identified previously; however, the current study aims to provide a comprehensive quantitative analysis of the issue using the fitting algorithm for the line-profiles of the Ca II H&K lines, specifically aiming to determine the existence of magnetic fields parallel to the line-of-sight, Bpar. The existence of magnetic fields parallel to the line-of-sight causes the model's optimisation process to result in biased estimates of the magnetic field strength and asymmetry. The study conducts a Fourier decomposition of the line profiles and uses the Fourier phases and power to estimate Bperp and Bpar. The Fourier phase provides a natural zero-point, eliminating the need for zero-point adjustment in the context of magnetic field strength. The study conducts a Fourier decomposition of the Line-Profile Index (LPI) and the Power of the Line-Profile (PLP) to achieve this. The results demonstrate that the Fourier decomposition technique reduces the bias in the estimation of Bpar. The study also establishes statistical relationships between the zero-point shift and bias, specifically a negative correlation with the Fourier phase. The technique is further tested using synthetic data.

This research paper explores a real-world scenario in which consumers selfishly aim to minimize their energy bills by scheduling their energy usage in advance. To effectively persuade these consumers to use less energy during peak hours and fairly compensate them, we developed a novel billing scheme that instantiates real-time energy usage charges. Initially, we define an aggregative game to simulate how these consumers strategically interact with one another. By employing variational inequality theory and the alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM), we devised two iterative algorithms that converge to the equilibrium state. To enhance efficiency, we also analyzed and implemented a substantially lighter alternative method with only three steps. Experimentation results demonstrate the performance superiority of our proposed billing scheme over Time-of-Use and Linear Pricing methods.

The generalized form of the Hawking temperature for charged and rotating black strings is confirmed using the tetrad formalism. Using the Hawking temperature, we examine the thermodynamic properties of these black strings in their most generalized form. Next, we confirm the first law of thermodynamics for these black strings with both rotational and magnetic components. Finally, we discuss the stability of these black strings under unstable conditions.

The results demonstrate that the power-law decay rates found in von Neumann's Ergodic Theorem for discrete systems directly correspond to pointwise scaling rates of a spectral measure with a spectral value of one. Moreover, assuming weak convergence, when no spectral gap is present, the convergence rates of the time-average in von Neumann's Ergodic Theorem rely on sequences of infinite time as they tend to infinity.

The research on extremely old and metal-poor stars within our Galaxy is instrumental in grasping its chemical development and the origin of star formation. These stars of great theoretical significance are rare, are typically identified through wide and shallow astronomical surveys, and then studied in depth. Following the successful identification of nine new carbon stars of very old population through a recent astronomical observation, this report outlines the discovery of two additional extremely old and metal-poor stars, bringing the total number of identified old carbon stars to eleven. Among these, nine are considered to be very old and metal-poor. The observation data of these stars have been gathered from the Gaia space observatory, and the analysis data collected through multi-aperture and high-resolution spectroscopic instruments. The study provides the first measurement of luminosity and temperature for these stars, and the temperature measurements are based on novel spectral lines specifically identified for old and metal-poor stars. The analysis data indicate that these stars possess very low metallic content equivalent to about a tenth of the content found in the sun, and the mass of the old and metal-poor stars range from three to half a ton. The discovery of the old and metal-poor stars has further widened the spread of temperatures and luminosity of the old carbon stars, and the study suggests that these stars of very old population may belong to two different categories of the old and metal-poor stars.

This research splits the Earth into a grid of hexagonal cells to collect and analyze worldwide data on daily fire counts from each cell for nearly two decades. The primary findings suggest that the majority of the globe experiences fire seasons lasting no more than eleven months, and approximately eighty-five percent of regions experience such short seasons. However, a few regions are susceptible to prolonged fire seasons, lasting up to almost twelve months, that recur annually for multiple years. On the other hand, areas prone to limited and isolated annual fire seasons, lasting no more than ten to eleven months, are also common. Furthermore, regions experiencing short and limited fire seasons alternate with those prone to prolonged and extensive seasonal patterns. This study further discovers that areas dependent on these temporary and scattered fires frequently experience lower fire frequencies, higher humidity, and lower planetary dryness compared to those with prolonged and extensive seasonal patterns that involve higher fire frequencies, lower humidity, and higher planetary dryness. The analysis reveals that areas experiencing extended and extensive seasonal patterns tend to display alternating patterns of high and moderate fire risks. However, regions experiencing short and isolated annual fire seasons, largely dependent on these temporary and scattered fires, frequently exhibit varying levels of fire risk, ranging from low to high.

We've conducted a thorough examination of eight distinct methods for evaluating the morphological intricacy of languages. These measures have different prerequisites for data annotation, yet our study identifies both similarities and disparities among them. We compare the methods visually and statistically to ascertain how they correlate with typological characteristics. This investigation seeks to determine whether these metrics assess the same underlying aspect of language or, alternatively, measure different facets of morphological complexity. The results from principal component analysis suggest that a substantial portion of variation across the eight measures is linearly associated.

Orphan stars discovered near the Milky Way's center can serve as proxies for the density and velocity dispersion of the surrounding stellar environment at their discovery site.  Using the Orphan Hunter pipeline, a search for these stars was conducted in a region 15-25 degrees from the far side of the Galaxy's center.  17 such stars were found, with 8 being previously unidentified, and an additional 9 drawn from a prior publication.  These stellar orbits were used to investigate the density of the surrounding interstellar medium at their discovery site.  Orphan stars moving at a velocity less than 130 km per second, and with an angular radius of 10 seconds, provide an estimate of the density of the surrounding gas and old population of the stellar disk.  Orphan stars moving at a velocity greater than 130 km per second, and with an angular radius greater than 10 seconds, provide an estimate of the density of the surrounding gas.  Orphan stars demonstrate a relationship between angular radius and velocity of the stellar disk at the Galactic center, with a steep decrease in density beyond a certain radius.  Orphan stars moving at a velocity greater than 130 km per second demonstrate a relationship between angular radius, independent of the stellar disk.
