A statistical analysis of 1.3 mm continuum cores from the Dragon infrared dark cloud reveals an interesting disparity between cores associated with molecular outflows, specifically protostellar and starless cores.  Protostellar cores are found to possess greater mass than their starless counterparts, with mass discrepancies holding true even after controlling for factors like temperature and size.  Further investigation of the core mass distribution indicates that the majority of mass resides within protostellar cores, despite starless cores exhibiting a broader mass range.  This contrast suggests that outflows are indicative not only of outflow activity, but also of mass.  As a result, future core surveys should be evaluated not only for outflow activity, but also for their inherent mass characteristics.

The theoretical primordial black holes that may have formed in the early universe are proposed as a possible type of dark matter. If these black holes exist, they can potentially be identified through specific star-related signals resulting from gravitational lensing. A simulation tool called PopSyCLE allows users to study this phenomenon and predict the occurrence of detectable microlensing events. In this study, we applied PopSyCLE to analyze 20 years of data from the Kepler telescope, searching for signs of SMBH-related star formation driven by gravitational lensing. As a result, we found no statistically significant occurrences of SMBH-related star formation, setting new limits for the abundance of primordial black holes in the universe with a mass between $10^{10}$ and $10^{13}$ solar masses. These restrictions are more stringent than existing ones for this range of masses. In particular, our study has yielded the tightest limits on primordial black hole abundance with an upper mass bound of $2.0 \times 10^{-3}\,M_\odot\,\mathrm{Mpc}^{-3}$ at $10^{12.5}$ solar masses. This has also resulted in the first-ever constraints on black hole decay caused by dark matter, specifically on the product of the dark matter particle's decay width and mass, denoted $\Gamma_\chi\,\Delta\rho_\chi$, which has an upper bound of approximately $10^{-7}\,\mathrm{GeV}$ for a mass range of $

We conducted research into systems at equilibrium consisting of uniform wedge-shaped molecules using Monte Carlo simulations, where each molecule consisted of six aligned spheres of gradually decreasing sizes, and the shape of these molecules was defined solely by the ratio of the smallest to the largest sphere diameters, referred to as parameter 'a' in the study. The systems studied involved varying numbers of molecules within square-vault nanomaterial structures and of five distinct flexibility gradients spanning from sharp to rounded shapes (where $a = 0.1, 0.5, 1, 5,$ and $ 10$). The systems were put into five distinct flexible gradients spanning from sharp to rounded shapes (where $a = 1/10, 1/5, 1, 5,$ and $ 10$). The systems were put into uniform simulations the results of which showed 6 distinct long order and phase structures from molecules with flexibility gradients and temperature as shown in the main text of the study. The study explored the relationship between molecular flexibility, temperature, and geometry gradients and their effect on 6 distinct long order and phase gradients. Our goal with parameter-efficient tuning is to minimize updates to model parameters
when adapting a pre-trained model to downstream tasks. This paper proposes PASTA,
where we adjust only the special token embeddings, like separator tokens, and special
representations. For tasks like classification, we use the classifier token to produce
logits directly. The PASTA framework can be applied efficiently with as little as one
optimization step per token type. Experiment results across various tasks on GLUE and
SuperGLUE show that PASTA achieves competitive performance with existing techniques,
such as fine-tuning and hyperparameter optimization methods like SLIM, while requiring
much faster training times. For example, on the IMDB dataset for text classification,
PASTA achieves similar accuracy after 3 steps as fine-tuning after 100 iterations.

This paper investigates a complex problem where we need to assess the impact of adding items to a collection. The inherent nature of this problem prevents us from making absolute preferences between options, which prompts the use of context-dependent preference modeling. To tackle this issue, we examine two distinct Siamese network designs, contrasting one that compares the resultant collections after an addition with another that considers each item's individual contribution to the existing collection. Through experiments involving a real-world task of learning Magic: The Gathering deck-building card preferences, we found that the triplet network outperformed its counterpart and surpassed previous performance levels in this area.

Our application of the lattice cluster theory for polymer fluids has established that the configurational entropy, enthalpy, and internal energy are interconnected thermodynamic properties that vary jointly with temperature. However, traditional versions of the lattice cluster model separate these components, leading to inconsistent results when these properties are simultaneously varied during simulations aimed at modeling glassy and soft amorphous phases. To address this limitation, we developed a single-body version of the lattice cluster model that merges the entropy, enthalpy, and internal energy terms and retains the existing interactions between monomers, carbons, and voids. This new version of the lattice cluster model maintains the chemical specificity of the original LCL Potassium carbonate, and its assessments against glassy and soft amorphous blends of potassium carbonate and polyethylene glycol demonstrate accuracy by matching experimentally determined glass transition temperatures and showing improved agreement with molecular dynamics simulations.

Transformer-based language models have been shown to struggle with logical reasoning, especially when it involves negation. Unlike previous studies that relied on psycholinguistic tools, our research delves into types of negation from developmental psychology. We examine this knowledge gap through a natural language inference task by creating a set of specialized questions from existing NLI datasets, which helps us assess a range of models' ability to process these negation types. Our analysis indicates models perform notably well on some negation categories, revealing a substantial distinction in their handling of this information.

In neural machine translation, the attention model is now an integral component, enabling selective focusing on source sentence parts to predict target words. However, research reveals that target word generation depends not only on source sentences, but also heavily on previous generated target words, including distant words that can be difficult to model using traditional recurrent neural networks. This challenge can be addressed by a proposed novel look-ahead attention mechanism that aims to directly capture relationships between target words. We further explore the integration of our mechanism with conventional attention to enhance its performance by sharing parameters with a transformer-based setup, ultimately demonstrating significant gains on various NMT benchmarks in both speed and performance.

This passage provides an in-depth, explicit calculation for the weights of Kontsevich graphs that emerge from connections and curvatures within a symplectic manifold framework, specifically focusing on globalization. We'll demonstrate how curvature graph weights can be explicitly defined through a hypergeometric function and an even simpler expression that combines it with a formula for the underlying connection graph weights. Notably, we examine a cotangent bundle case, leading to a substantial simplification of the curvature expression.

This research involves determining the large N limit of $O(N)$ models with non-polynomial potential functions in odd dimensional spaces, leading to a new class of interacting conformal field theories. Specifically, this results in CFTs for dimensions 3+4n where n is a positive integer. Calculations of thermal entropy are also carried out for these same dimensions and time periods. It was discovered that in two dimensions, entanglement entropy within the vacuum state is constant for large N limits, while for dimensions above 2 it scales in proportion to N. This phenomenon could potentially be explained by a previously established relationship discovered by Giudice, Karski and Rattazzi. Moreover, this study's thermal entropy results align with the Scaramazza and Viñas' formula for thermal entropy.

Cai, Song and Kou made a significant contribution in 2015 with the development of a universal approach for pricing Asian options based on one-dimensional Markov processes. This note applies the CTMC framework, calculating the inverse Z-transform and inverse Laplace transform separately for discretely and continuously monitored options. As a result, we achieve improved explicit Laplace transforms, surpassing a prior theorem by Cai et al. and yielding increased efficiency through numerical studies.

The diffuse gamma-ray background can be explained in part by unobserved Galactic objects, such as old brown dwarfs, and star clusters. To explore the possibility of contributing to the background, researchers examined the gamma-ray properties of supernova-remnant-embedded clusters, specifically G8.0-1.0 and Sagittarius A East. These clusters, embedded within supernova remnants, have high star densities and massive pulsar winds, and are located near the Galactic center, respectively. Using the Fermi Gamma Ray Space Telescope, researchers searched for gamma-ray emissions from these clusters, and their analysis revealed no significant findings. However, researchers did detect a gamma-ray signal from G8.0-1.0, likely produced by hadronic interactions between cosmic rays and the supernova-remnant gas. The absence of a gamma-ray signal from Sagittarius A East could be due to reduced alchemy or specific magnetic-field orientations. Additionally, researchers set upper limits for gamma-ray production at specific energy levels for both clusters, and estimated that hadronic processes account for a substantial fraction, around 20-50%, of the diffuse gamma-ray background. Specifically, they found that Galactic supernova-remnant-embedded clusters contribute around 11-24% of the background.

Extra energy injected by primordial features in inflationary models can generate massive particles exceeding GeV in weight, providing a potential explanation for the dark matter phenomenon. Although the resulting particles are extremely rare, their collisions with standard model particles produce noticeable signatures due to their substantial cross-sections. These signatures become evident through the creation of particles like $J/\psi$, $\mu^+\mu^-$, and $Z$-bosons, especially in detector environments where cosmic radiation is measured, distinguishing them from terrestrial signals by their spatial distribution and alignment with 91-degree large-scale anisotropy $\mu^+\mu^-$ signs. Observing these signatures with future experiments, such as Fermi-LAT and KM3NeT, could confirm models incorporating primordial features that generate massive particles, especially with temperatures below 100 GeV.

Understanding how complex visual models work is crucial, and developing techniques to explain these models can be particularly challenging. To address this issue, a framework called LaViSE is proposed to enable convolutional neural networks to describe their internal workings in plain text. By using generic image data, this approach creates a link between visual and semantic information, allowing for its application across different domains without explicit labels. The LaViSE framework has been put to the test on two artificial tasks, which involved unseen product images and building blocks of everyday objects, resulting in accurate explanations that matched user expectations. Despite its limitations when dealing with real-world scenarios, this approach opens up new possibilities for future research.

Developing a simplified microscopic model of cuprates is crucial in uncovering the mechanism behind high-temperature superconductivity. By comparing our simulation results with a recent photoemission spectroscopy study of one-dimensional cuprate chains, we have discovered that long-range electron-phonon coupling plays a crucial role in shaping electron interactions. Within reasonable limits of this interaction, our model yields a Fermi liquid ground state with superconductivity emerging from electron-phonon mediation, consistent with experimental observations. However, when the conduction electron confinement is too strong, a charge 2 superconducting state arises instead. Notably, our analysis implies a critical need for direct and indirect measurements of cuprate band structures.

The ongoing HIV epidemic remains a pressing concern around the world. Although, in recent years, there have been significant advancements in understanding the virus, a considerable segment of population still remains unaware of HIV. Understanding the causes of HIV awareness across different segments of population is crucial, as it can aid in developing targeted campaigns and programs to disseminate information to those in need. In this research paper, we examine HIV awareness across various subgroups of the Indian population, utilizing a comprehensive typer of data that tracks online activity as well as offline surveys related to HIV. Our analysis reveals distinct patterns of HIV awareness across different age groups, where younger individuals exhibit higher awareness of the virus compared to their older counterparts. Furthermore, our findings indicate that educational levels, as reported by government records, are positively correlated with HIV awareness, suggesting that socioeconomic factors play a significant role. Interestingly, our data shows that awareness of HIV prevention methods is prevalent among women, whereas awareness of the virus itself is prevalent among men. Our statistical analysis not only confirms these observations but also uncovers additional insights, as we employ a range of techniques, including copulas, which are statistical tools to analyze multivariate data. Our findings suggest that socioeconomic factors, including a woman's age and education level, are effective indicators of HIV awareness in designing programs and interventions.

In the chiral magnet Co$_9$Zn$_9$Mn$_2$ of $\beta$-Mn type, it's discovered that the previously unknown phase, called 3D modulated structure, exhibits topological skyrmion lattice characteristics, confirmed through various symmetry analysis methods. Using sensitive techniques, it's found that this unique phase emerges when cooling below 20 Kelvin and persists up to 25 Kelvin, coexisting with the previously known long-range ordered ferromagnetic state. A close examination using X-ray scattering and neutron diffraction reveals fine modulations within the ferromagnetic state, signifying its underlying complex structure. This intriguing material offers valuable opportunities for studying the interplay between long-range and short-range magnetic order, which is unique at the large scale.

High-Dimensional Dynamic Factor Models are thoroughly explored, covering key 
assumptions and their underlying rationales, significant outcomes, and example
exhibits through simple demonstrations. The theory and implementation of 
these models, focusing specifically on singular ARMA models, is examined. The 
paper prioritizes detailing model types over methodology and results.

The equilibrium problem described by the Nikaid\^o-Isoda-Fan inequality encompasses several key problems like optimization, variational inequality, and others, as specific instances. This paper aims to provide a clear outline illustrating the connection between fixed points of the Moreau proximal mapping and solutions to the equilibrium problem that satisfy particular monotonicity and Lipschitz-type constraints.

Recent breakthroughs in deep learning have brought about a significant transformation in the field of reversible steganography. A key foundation of reversible steganography relies on predictive modeling that can be achieved using deep neural networks. However, critical inaccuracies persist when dealing with data outside the scope of a model, known as out-of-distribution (OOD) data. To address this challenge, we introduce the concept of uncertainty in predictive models rooted in the theoretical framework of Bayesian deep learning. Bayesian neural networks can be viewed as probabilistic ensembles of weight configurations, each capable of forming predictions. By disentangling epistemic uncertainty (a lack of information about an object or scene) and intrinsically uncertain data (true OOD data), we develop an effective method for accurately identifying OOD images. This innovative approach unlocks the potential for dynamic steganalytic properties and reversible steganography protocols. Experimental findings reveal our uncertainty-based classifier to boast superior area under the receiver operating characteristic with distances ranging from 0.083 to 0.135, compared to current state-of-the-art methods spanning a range from 0.075 to 0.162.

The debate on turbulent effects influencing magnetic activity in the Sun and stars persists. The mean-field theory provides a widely applied framework to link these effects to fundamental magnetohydrodynamics, although it's not possible to observe these effects directly. To gain insight, researchers utilize global dynamo simulations to understand and quantify the impact of turbulent forces. A novel study employs multiple global dynamo simulations with varying magnetic configurations and rotational histories to estimate and compare turbulent transport coefficients across different scenarios. These simulations reveal significant variations in coefficients when comparing pure barotropic vs baroclinic flows and when rotating rates change. The results suggest that coefficients measured in simulations are highly dependent on the specific dynamo model used and magnetic and fluid configurations, making general applications and extensions challenging.

A study has revealed molecular outflows in the central area of the galaxy NGC4945 using the ALMA. At a high resolution of ~0.3", the ALMA detected four distinct plumes of molecular gas, possibly corresponding to gas situated at the edges of an existing ionized outflow. Observations of line-of-sight velocities exceeding 450 km/s indicate outflow velocities exceeding 600 km/s in the fastest emitting plume. Most of these molecular gas outflows have counterparts in the emissions of HCN and HCO+. A proposed model suggests the molecular gas outflows have a cone-like geometry similar to ionized outflows and share the galaxy's rotation velocity when expelled. Using this model, it's possible to calculate the speed of ejected material and account for unobserved outflows that may be obscured. It's estimated that about 20% of the galaxy's water supply is expelled with outflows that contain a significant amount of this molecule, possibly as a result of star-formation or an active galactic nucleus.

A simplified version of the original Vlasov-Maxwell equations for magnetized plasmas is provided by quasilinear theory, describing how particles interact with waves through resonant processes. The reduced model in a turbulent regime shows that the distribution of particles changes over time due to wave-particle interaction, with the distribution function becoming multiply connected. The paper derives a practical method for numerically simulating this phenomenon using magnetic reconnection as an example, with the goal of understanding how it affects particle diffusion. The diffusion resulting from the multiple connections in the distribution function is analyzed, with the focus on its impact on particle diffusion rates, with the results compared to full Vlasov simulations. The paper shows that the quasilinear model is capable of accurately modeling particle diffusion in a magnetized plasma under specific conditions.

Previous variable stepsize Second Derivative General Linear Methods have already been implemented using the Nordsieck technique, and we extend this work by directly introducing variable stepsize SGLMs onto non-uniform grids. We then establish order conditions for these new methods of order p with q=p stage order and demonstrate them through specific examples up to order four, further confirming their efficiency in solving non-stiff problems via successful test cases.

We provide a relationship between the exponential stability of a C0-semigroup T and solutions of a specific Lyapunov inequality in B+(X,X*), where X is a Banach space. The inequality's solutions determine the boundedness of the resolvent R(λ,A) inside and outside the left half-plane and left invertibility of T, the C0-semigroup.

This paper introduces MuMuPy, a computational software and web-based tool for determining the interaction cross sections between matter and dimuonium (true polonium), muonium, and other muon-containing compounds. By utilizing such tools, researchers working on muon-based experiments can assess potential muon-based backgrounds in those investigations. Cross checks with established literature are also performed, as described in the accompanying web note.

Portfolio managers assess investment success in relation to market standards, specifically using the Standard & Poor 500 index as a benchmark. Our model, built in R, calculates and analyzes portfolio performance relative to this benchmark, considering various market benchmarks and timeframes. This R package, PerformanceAnalysis, allows users to specify the benchmark and timeframe via the 'performance' function, producing a list with the main performance indicators. Key metrics include the portfolio's annualized return, volatility, skewness, kurtosis, Sortino ratio, Sharpe ratio, and Sortino and Sharpe ratios relative to the benchmark. Moreover, the 'plotPerformance' function generates a graphic displaying these ratios. For a single-period analysis, the 'performanceTable' function creates a table summarizing portfolio performance. Additionally, the 'performanceMultiple' function is utilized to calculate a portfolio's performance for a specified number of time periods and 'plotPerformanceMultiple' for the associated graphic.

The most abundant galaxy type in the cosmos is dwarf galaxies, which exhibit distinct characteristics when compared to larger, brighter counterparts. This research focuses on the physical and chemical properties of the interstellar material within dwarf galaxies. This study employed the 3D model modeler3d to create three-dimensional models of the interstellar gas and dust observed in the nearby dwarf galaxies DDO 154 and NGC 5253. Using observations from the Herschel Space Observatory, the study determined the gas and dust properties across these galaxies. The research found a positive correlation between gas and dust levels and a specific star formation rate indicator in both test subjects. However, the study also uncovered a discrepancy between gas and dust levels and a specific star formation rate indicator in some regions of NGC 5253. The analysis suggested that this divergence might be the result of either dust being radiatively accelerated or gas being photo-evaporated. This study implies that both gas and dust are efficiently converted into stars within these galaxies. The study further provides evidence that both gas and dust are effectively converted into stars over a limited period in some areas of NGC 5253, possibly as a result of a gas collapse triggered by a black hole disturbance in the test subject.

We examine the stability of fermionic quasiparticles in a fermion-boson model based on a Bethe lattice, where fermions interact with local bosons through a Peierls coupling. By reducing the complex model into a non-interacting chain with varying site potentials, we demonstrate that despite interactions with bosons, fermions retaining half bandwidths exhibit minimal disruption in behavior. Specifically, a plot of quasiparticle weight versus bandwidth reveals that quasiparticle stability is protected at specific points, such as $e^{-2j\pi /3}$, $e^{-2j\pi /4}$, and $e^{-2j\pi /5}$. These points signify where the phase of $\lambda_m$ changes, effectively capturing the transition from repulsive to attractive interactions between bosons and fermions. Furthermore, a scaling bootstrap study of two-point fermion correlations in the lattice model reveals that in the thermodynamic limit, the largest energy scale $\lambda_M$ yields the dominant correlation, potentially leading to a quantum critical point at $\lambda_M = e^{-j\pi /2}$.

Golan and Sapir \cite{MR3978542} showed that the Thompson's groups $F$, $T$, and $V$ exhibit linear divergence. The present work extends this analysis to broader classes of these groups. Specifically, we investigate the Brown-Thompson groups $F_n$, $T_n$, and $V_n$ and discover that they too have a linear divergence function. Furthermore, our research encompasses the braided Thompson groups $BF$, $\widehat{BF}$, and $\widehat{BV}$. Alongside existing results in \cite{Kodama:2020to}, our findings confirm that these braided groups display linear divergence as well.

This paper demonstrates the end-to-end fine-tuning of the Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) architecture. Key to RAG's flexibility and strength is its ability to seamlessly integrate with both external knowledge retrieval and text generation. However, achieving this requires a well-designed architecture that can effectively combine these components. Contrary to the original RAG architecture, which requires the pre-training of separate retrieval and generation components before application to specific NLP tasks, our research involves the detailed process of fine-tuning the architecture in an end-to-end capacity. A RAG architecture fine-tuned in this capacity exhibits impressive results on the QA tasks, surpassing the performance of the original RAG architecture. Furthermore, our RAG architecture fine-tuned in the end-to-end capacity also facilitates the incorporation of multiple knowledge passages drawn from various external sources, thereby significantly enhancing its overall performance. Multiple experiments have been conducted to investigate the RAG architecture fine-tuned in the end-to-end capacity, including analysis of the impact of the architecture's various components, such as the use of multiple knowledge passages and a dual-stage generation process. A public implementation of the architecture is also available for reference.

This study calculates the long-term behavior of the recurrence coefficients for polynomials that are orthogonal in relation to a specific logarithmic weight given by $\log\left(\frac{2k}{1-x}\right)$ over the interval $(-1,1)$ where $k>1$, and we verify a long-standing conjecture of A. Magnus regarding these coefficients, making use of the Riemann-Hilbert and steepest descent methods in an unconventional manner since no solution to the R-H problem exists in the classical sense due to the non-analytic nature of the problem.

Utilizing crowdsourcing platforms like Amazon Mechanical Turk to acquire top-tier human annotations proves more complicated than initially thought, influenced by several key factors, such as task instructions and annotator compensation, among others. To prevent inaccurate annotations which could mislead automatic summarization systems, we develop a multi-stage recruitment process targeting high-quality MTurk workers. By establishing a rigorous evaluation pipeline, we demonstrate the ability to exclude unskilled workers before evaluation tasks are initiated, resulting in significantly improved annotation reliability. Specifically, our approach yields consistent 90% accuracy across diverse evaluation datasets and demonstrates cost-effectiveness through strategic worker selection and compensation optimization. Notably, our approach facilitates the discovery of novel, unannotated datasets that lie outside the reach of conventional recruitment methods.

Recent advances in vision-language tasks have highlighted the significance of semantic semantic relationships. This study presents TS2-Net, a unique framework that leverages token-level associations to enhance semantic coherence, and proposes a new correlation learning approach for visual recognition tasks. The architecture comprises a token shifting module where adjacent tokens with strong connections to assist correct classification are moved and reordered. The concept is incorporated into a transformer-based model called TS2-Net, consisting of a pre-shifting encoding module, token shifting module, and post-shifting decoding module. Evaluations on multiple image classification tasks demonstrate that TS2-Net yields superior performance and achieves state-of-the-art results on large-scale datasets such as ImageNet, ImageNet-21k, and NoCaps, while setting a new benchmark on the ReImAg-21k dataset.

We've found that neutral flavour-changing currents in top sector physics, linked to electroweak scale particles that interact with leptons, can appear naturally in new physics scenarios, especially in composite Higgs theories. It's been shown that existing experiments provide no restrictions on these interactions, but they can potentially be detected at the Large Hadron Collider by looking at rare top decays and in other processes involving top particles, leptons, and additional jets. Specifically, our analyses reveal that, given the appropriate conditions and an adequate dataset, it should be possible to detect effects from flavour-violating neutral currents that involve sub-10 GeV leptophilic scalars, even if their couplings with tops and leptons are relatively weak, below a threshold of 10^-7 and 10^-9, respectively, for certain masses of the scalar particles.

In response to the intricacies of network data, a new type of hybrid network is suggested that blends rules for preferential attachment and uniform attachment.  This hybrid network creates edges according to a mixture of these rules.  Specifically, when a new edge is added, it follows the preferential attachment rule with a certain probability and otherwise forms between two randomly selected nodes.  This approach leads to a distribution of node in- and out-degrees that has less extreme outliers compared to a purely preferential attachment network, thereby improving upon this traditional model.  Inference methods applicable to the new model are then explored and demonstrated with both artificially generated and actual network data, revealing the potential benefits of incorporating this flexible hybrid network into the study of real-world networks where such less extreme outcomes are typically observed.

The expanding utilization of unlicensed frequency bands necessitates dependable interference management systems and hence reliable identification of wireless interference (WII). Our research proposes a novel WII technique that uses a deep convolutional neural network to accurately identify multiple co-channel interference signals (from IEEE 802.15.1, IEEE 802.11 b/g and IEEE 802.15.4) amidst a background noise process or other interfering signals. The created multi-task learning approach enhances the identification accuracy of each signal type. By leveraging a deep neural network, this method bypasses the need for a detailed channel model and achieves strong interference detection and signal recognition. To facilitate rapid deployment, we provide a comprehensive comparison of the proposed algorithm's performance using various datasets.

To grasp the impact of gravitational forces on both quantum systems moving at varying speeds and stationary systems, we must rely on two key theories: Quantum Mechanics and General Relativity. Although these theories challenge each other, we can find common ground by applying the Schrödinger-Newton equation, which shows that gravitational forces significantly affect quantum energy levels. In this context, we develop the Quantum Causal Graph Formulation, which incorporates time-like and space-like edges representing the coupling of quantum systems to gravitational fields, thereby accurately describing Quantum Mechanics within the frameworks of both Schrödinger-Newton and Dirac-Einstein equations. This formulation allows us to model complex networks of quantum systems coupled to various sources of gravity. By extending the graph formulation to encompass distributed gravitational fields and coupling mechanisms, we bridge the gap between General Relativity and Quantum Mechanics, providing a unified understanding of quantum systems coupled to various sources of gravity.
Countable, locally standard measure algebras are parameterized by a pair of Steinitz numbers, consisting of one value which equals or exceeds 1.

Parton distributions that account for quark and gluon correlations within a nucleon can be understood through generalized parton distributions. Research focuses on extracting GPDs from experimental data collected in experiments involving both elastic electron-nucleon scattering and various electron-jet processes. Additionally, theoretical calculations consider GPDs in the context of nucleon rotation, deformation, and the resulting changes in parton momenta. These calculations are based on the light-front holographic wavefunctions of bound nucleons derived from light-front quantum chromodynamics principles. The study also analyzes the effect of nucleon rotation on GPDs in detail. Results indicate significant changes in parton momenta during the nucleon's rotation rotation, which in turn affect the behavior of both the skewness and parton distribution slopes as a function of the off-shell parameter Delta. Furthermore, the study finds that the nucleon's rotation impacts the behavior of the parton distribution function a(x, Delta) significantly at large-x values when Delta is positive and at small-x values when Delta is negative. This has the effect of increasing the parton distribution slopes at large-x and decreasing them at small-x when the nucleon's rotation is taken into account.

All AI systems inevitably make mistakes, characterized by their unpredictability. A unique approach to addressing these errors involves directing the AI to clarify or correct its own responses. However, the cost of implementing this method through human intervention is counteracted when its implementation is feasible and affordable. A new system was designed to overcome this limitation, utilizing a combination of automated tools, including a custom interface and automated processing systems, to identify and correct AI-induced errors. As evidenced by user testing, this approach was found to be effective in educating the AI to produce more accurate results. Moreover, user feedback indicated that one of the most valuable benefits of this system was the transfer of knowledge, enabling the AI to produce better results in other tasks as well.

Our research involves exploring the thermal behavior of the Bose-Hubbard model in the presence of strong spin-orbit coupling originating from a mean-field state. By introducing a spin-orbit coupling factor γ, we observe the emergence of finite-wavevector condensation of bosons. The superfluid properties of the system can manifest as homogeneous superfluid or exhibit a logarithmic divergence in density with distance, depending on the strength of γ. As γ increases, the threshold for the superfluid-Mott insulator transition in the model shifts towards smaller interaction parameters. Additionally, we investigate the effect of γ on the thermal transitions in the model. For the superfluid-Mott insulator transition, we found that increasing γ causes it to shift towards smaller interaction parameters, splitting it into multiple transitions at approximately log(γ) = 2, 3, 4.

Consider two groups, G_1 and G_2, and suppose a homomorphism \phi from G_1 to G_2 maps a particular element to another element. In the context of graph theory, this leads to the concept of a group G_1 degrading to group G_2, which is investigated in this paper. Graph degeneration is explored as a specific instance of this group relationship. The study focuses on categories with a product, has a closed under composition and inverse properties, and uses category theory to describe graph degeneration as a group relationship. It demonstrates that different categories result in various notions of graph degeneration, and examines categories corresponding to different graph substitution systems.

Recent breakthroughs in AdS/CFT correspondence research, specifically in low-dimensional settings, are examined, concentrating on AdS$_3$/CFT$_2$ and AdS$_2$/CFT$_1$ dualities from massive Type IIA string theory. We first explore solutions from the work of Seiberg and Witten that encompass both 3d and 2d supersymmetric gauge theories. Next, solutions derived by Gubser, Maldacena, Gupta and Sulach that incorporate 3d and 2d components are analyzed. Notably, these formulations offer dual pairs featuring non-Abelian and Abelian components in both the AdS$_3$/CFT$_2$ and AdS$_2$/CFT$_1$ frameworks. A detailed analysis of the dual pairs involving non-Abelian components in AdS$_3$/CFT$_2$ is provided, along with an assessment of the known constraints from the holographic principle in both the gauge theory and supergravity sectors. We also present a case for the application of the non-Abelian version of the holographic duality principle. Additionally, the paper includes an investigation of the proposal by Brede, Fiol and Trunin on non-Abelian holographic duality, along with key results from the supergravity component that have been overlooked in existing literature.

In numerous Machine Learning applications, selecting an optimal covariance function, also known as a kernel, is a crucial step, largely influenced by its parameters. Gaussian Processes hold vast potential in this area. A new study demonstrates the viability of a Genetic-Programming approach in automatically determining the most suitable Gaussian Process kernel. By leveraging this method, Gaussian Processes can efficiently handle complex problems from diverse domains with previously unachievable precision. Additionally, the approach enables Gaussian Processes to seamlessly address challenging tasks such as multi-objective optimization, time-series forecasting, and high-dimensional, massive-data analysis, ultimately bridging the gap between supervised and unsupervised learning.

Future high-energy muon colliders face a challenge due to in-flight decays of
muons from the beam line, resulting in beam-induced backgrounds (BIB). This
background interference will hinder accurate data analysis and detector
operation unless mitigated. Research focuses on reducing BIB in detector systems
targeting the 1 GeV to 10 GeV energy range, with results including findings
for the SHiP experiment utilizing a Cherenkov detector and an electromagnetic
calorimeter. In the same BIB energy band, findings also regarding a calorimeter
sensitive to all particle types are presented. Additionally, an energy range
analysis for BIB in intensity-modulated proton beams is conducted.

Introducing Spartan, a novel approach for training neural networks with pre-defined sparsity. This method effectively leverages a combination of two techniques: soft parameter pruning through optimal transportation and hard parameter sparsification during forward passes. This dynamic balance enables initial exploration of various sparsity patterns and gradually shifts towards optimizing parameters with respect to a predetermined sparsity pattern. Spartan offers flexibility in incorporating diverse sparsity policies, encompassing both random and structured sparsity, as well as cost-sensitive allocation guided by per-parameter training targets. Spartan demonstrates exceptional performance on ImageNet-1K classification, achieving significant sparsity in ResNet-50 and ViT-B/16 models while maintaining accuracy within 1% of their fully dense counterparts.

The intricate connection between many-body interactions and the spatial dimension of a system plays a pivotal role in determining its behavior. A crucial aspect of this relationship is the influence of spatial constraints on the thermalization of interacting gases. A one-dimensional Bose gas is renowned for its soliton-like properties, which significantly affect its thermodynamic characteristics. Through the application of the soliton-lattice representation, coupled with a perturbative analysis, it is demonstrated that one-dimensional Bose gases do not fully thermalize in the general sense. Instead, system states are characterized by complex superpositions of solitons, with lattice structures, and long-distance correlations, all maintained at non-equilibrium levels even after prolonged evolution. Only when the lattice structures are sufficiently disrupted do soliton strips form, marking the extent to which thermalization occurs. High-perturbation levels result in the emergence of a soliton gas, while the system's phase fluctuations are described by complex solitons. Consequently, it is established that the convergence to thermal equilibrium is confined to the limits of high particle densities.

Software developers widely acknowledge the importance of unit testing as a crucial aspect of their work cycle, allowing for swift detection and resolution of coding errors. However, test code can be compromised by suboptimal design or implementation choices referred to as test smells. These shortcomings can significantly undermine the quality of software systems by exacerbating difficulties in comprehension, amplifying maintenance complexities, and making systems more susceptible to bugs and errors. Prior studies have investigated the likely consequences of test smells on test code. Despite their focus, a knowledge gap remains regarding the perspectives of developers regarding these issues. To bridge this knowledge gap, our research work aims to delve into software developers' perceptions of test smells and their impact. We conducted an in-depth investigation by conducting semi-structured interviews with 12 developers from three different software development companies, exploring their views on test smells, their effects, and how developers detect them. Based on these interviews, our analysis reveals that developers primarily identify test smells through code review, attribute their causes to style or functionality issues, and attempt to eliminate them. Furthermore, our results indicate that developers' awareness and detection of test smells vary in terms of complexity, duration of experience, and the specific smell in question. Finally, our study shows that developers' awareness regarding true test smells still lags behind their understanding of common design smells.

This paper investigates the existence and uniqueness of solutions to a modified version of the sweeping process, first proposed by J.J. Moreau in the early 1970s as part of plasticity theory. The proposed modification involves a novel combination of a geodesic integral variable structure framework and the Moreau integration-to-differential transform technique. In this revised framework, the ordinary differential equation includes a Carathéodory mapping and an integral forcing term that depends on two different time variables. Consequently, the paper demonstrates that the modified sweeping process can be viewed as a particular type of variable structure system. The text also provides examples of suitable applications of the proposed algorithm.

We introduce the updated version of the {\tt KKMCee} event generator, version 5.00.2, designed for simulating electron-positron collisions. This event generator is now integrated into the {\tt MadGraph5\_aMC@NLO} framework and incorporates the most recent Monte Carlo predictions outlined in the {\it Precision Studies at the Future e$^+$e$^-$ Colliders} report. The {\tt KKMCee} 5.00.2 includes precise calculations for four-fermion processes, gauge boson pair production, and vector boson fusion, all of which are determined at the Born, first order, and double order in $\alpha$ electromagnetic factors. The event generator also accounts for the full Standard Model treatment of fermion decays and interactions, as well as initial and final-state radiation. It offers the capability to account for beam polarisation, $\it{CP}$-violating phases, and electroweak corrections. The {\tt KKMCee} 5.00.2 event generator offers four simulation modes: 0$\gamma$ $Z$ $Z$ SIMULATION, which pairs $Z$'s; $Z$ $\gamma$ SIMULATION, pairing $Z$ with $\gamma$; $\gamma$ $\gamma$ SIMULATION, pairing $\gamma$ with $\gamma$; and VBF SIMULATION, implementing the vector boson fusion process. The chosen simulation mode dictates which processes are

Measuring inter-beat intervals from ECG signals can provide early warnings for cardiovascular diseases. However, identifying IBIs from noisy signals is difficult, especially when they are heavily distorted by motion noise, which is common in individuals who are highly active. Researchers working on remote health monitoring and wearable devices have identified signal denoising and IBI estimation as a significant area of interest. Recent breakthroughs have involved the employment of deep learning, which has shown remarkable capabilities in signal denoising and IBI estimation. This study presents a deep learning approach, referred to as VR-Watch, which utilizes a multi-task framework combining 1D and2D convolutional neural networks to simultaneously eliminate noise and recover IBIs from ECG signals. By producing accurate IBI estimates and quantifying signal cleaniness through HRV metrics, VR-Watch has excelled at IBI estimation and signal denoising, achieving the best records in the Lin et al. (2017) and Jelm\'{e}r et al. (2017) datasets.

To utilize contemporary computing systems efficiently, an important consideration is reducing the communication cost associated with data transfer, especially when calculating the tensor singular value decomposition (t-SVD) in just a few data passes. A recent research paper proposed by Zhou et al. in 2020, although innovative, actually reiterates an earlier idea from 2018 by Li et al., who both contended that a t-SVD can be obtained by applying the multi-level singular value decomposition (MLSVD) on reduced-order tensor submatrices, which are constructed from the original tensor through selective extraction of tensor elements. A t-SVD computed using this method may be incomplete; nonetheless, it correctly captures the rank of the tensor. A theoretical framework was developed to determine the accuracy of this incomplete t-SVD by establishing a relationship between the residual norm and the selected tensor elements' magnitude. Moreover, an adaptive method for determining the number of tensor elements to sample for computing the t-SVD was explored, sampling those elements with the greatest magnitude. The proposed strategies were demonstrated to be efficient both in theory and in experiments.

Network analytics heavily relies on embedding static graphs in low-dimensional vector spaces to enable node classification, link prediction, and visualization, but this approach has limitations when applied to dynamic networks with evolving nodes, edges, and attributes. To overcome these limitations, researchers have developed various techniques for dynamic graph embedding, which can accommodate these changes and provide embedded representations for each network snapshot or time step. These embeddings can then be combined using different methods to obtain a single representation for each node that captures its temporal evolution. In this paper, we provide a comprehensive survey on dynamic graph embedding, including existing algorithms, benchmark datasets, and popular evaluation metrics, as well as discuss the unresolved challenges in this field.

Our investigation into a $^7$H resonant state treated as a five-body system with a $^3$H core and four neutrons involved, involved constructing an effective neutron-$^3$H potential to reproduce phase shifts for neutron scattering on $^3$H, and to describe the $^5$H resonant ground state in a $^3$H-n-n configuration. Utilizing the Variational Gaussian Expansion Method to evolve the time-independent Schrödinger equation with this potential, we identified a additional resonance within the $^7$H energy range. We determined that the ground state configuration of this approximately 9 MeV wide resonance, situated about 5.3 (Eqs.) MeV above it, is a $^3$H-n-n-n-n-n cluster with quantum numbers 0$\leq$ $l_{H_n}$ $\leq$ 2, 2$\leq$ $l_{n_n}$ $\leq$ 3, and 0$\leq$ $l_{n_n}$ $\leq$ 2. This suggested structure is consistent with a macroscopically delocalized, quasi continuum state where one neutron is tightly bound in the $^3$H-n cluster and the remaining five neutrons are weakly coupled. Our study also found that the strength of the $^3$H-n potential significantly affects the $^7$H resonant state, whose structure transitions

This research paper investigates a Nirenberg type problem on a half-sphere: finding smooth solutions to an elliptic equation whose boundary conditions involve a source term. We demonstrate that solutions to a simplified version of this problem can develop singularities. However, despite having a source term with positive coefficients, the solutions do not avoid the boundary as they blow up. By contrasting the properties of the problem on a sphere with those on a half-sphere, we can explain this phenomenon. In the process, we identify a second family of solutions to the problem, the existence of which was previously unknown. These new solutions have properties analogous to those found in a half-disc and enable us to study their behavior as they approach the boundary using the blow-up method. This research provides the key to solving the problem and allows us to conclude that its solutions behave erratically near the boundary.

Deep Metric Learning methods primarily aim to develop a space where data similarities can be maintained. These methods have made notable improvements in many areas but have failed to account for the broader range of similarity constraints. As a result, suboptimal metrics in the embedded space have been the outcome. New approaches are proposed to overcome this limitation by incorporating constraints on the embedded space that reflect the full range of inter-data similarity differences. These additional constraints facilitate distinguishing similar data points while separating dissimilar ones. Experimental results show that incorporating these extra constraints leads to better embedded spaces, particularly for cases where data similarities are not sufficiently capturing key characteristics. The approach is referred to as Deep Similarity Expansion and can be applied as either distance regularization or a kernel-based method, with the simple implementation shown to outperform many existing state-of-the-art models.

In various fields of scientific inquiry, a common challenge exists in determining the effects of interventions on multiple types of outcomes.
To address this issue, we've developed a novel method which can efficiently handle a wide array of outcome types including binary, continuous, and categorical.
The approach relies on fitting distinct structural models to every possible combination of observed variables for each outcome type, with the objective of minimizing a calculated bias metric.
A versatile framework has been created to seamlessly integrate multiple models and outcomes, allowing for seamless adaptation to different scenarios.
Throughout this methodology, a type of outcome known as the "Bernoulli" is utilized; therefore, for cases involving mixed categorical outcome types, the ability to convert outcomes to their corresponding Bernoulli forms is essential.
With this approach, simulations have demonstrated that models are capable of achieving an optimal level of bias minimization.
Furthermore, the efficacy of this method has been successfully tested using real-world data from two distinct fields of study, one focusing on cardiovascular disease and the other on criminal behavior.

Determination of essential parameters for Melotte 72, a loose star association located 1031+/- 8 parsecs from Earth, was achieved through evaluating the common motion of its member stars. Out of 32 potential members, 19 single stars were found suitable for analyzing the association's motion. From radial velocity measurements, seven members exhibited common motion, with an association membership probability threshold set at 90%. The parameters for Melotte 72 were refined as follows: radial velocity, transverse velocity, and distance remained unchanged at 15.5 plus/minus 0.4 km/s, 16.2 plus/minus 0.6 km/s, and 1031 plus/minus 8 parsecs, respectively. The association's mean radial velocity was found to be 15.5 plus/minus 0.4 km/s, with an intrinsic radial velocity dispersion of 0.5 km/s. The parameters suggest that the Melotte 72 association resides in the Perseus molecular cloud.

Data analysis applications in medicine, cosmology, and materials science are witnessing growing interest in probabilistic excursion patterns. This research provides the first thorough examination and exploration of Betti numbers under the lens of probability, focusing on the likely behavior of these topological indicators in random geometric objects as their dimensions increase. A key aspect of this study is establishing strong laws governing normalized Betti numbers around mean values. Specifically, we delve into the probabilistic characteristics of extrema and singularities within random samples, as well as the pattern of extreme values in clutters of varying nature.

In robotics, determining camera positions is beneficial for both tasks and validation. Two popular techniques for camera pose estimation, deep learning-based approaches and traditional computationally expensive methods, are discussed. To combine the strengths of both, a novel camera pose estimation framework is proposed, consisting of two components: a CNN-based method that generates semi-protected data and a subsequent camera pose optimization step. Experimental results using synthetic data showcase a significant improvement in 2D pose accuracy and related 3D pose estimates in a real-world scenario.

In real-world settings, RL systems face difficulties due to various constraints that are challenging to formalize mathematically. For RL applications, it is crucial that agents remain aware of these constraints to ensure safe operation. This work aims to tackle this issue by seeking constraints that enable an RL agent to learn policies that are optimal while adhering to predefined safety protocols. In doing so, it is proposed that a set of safety-related constraints can be derived through inverse reinforcement learning methods, that are initially applied to a agent's historical data. This agent then utilizes model-based machine learning techniques to create a predictive model, that is trained on past data. This approach has the benefit of being capable of generalizing to unseen situations without the need for explicit demonstration of safety scenarios. Ultimately, this method has the potential to reduce the amount of manually defined safety protocols required during training. Experimental findings indicate significant performance enhancements when using learned safety constraints compared to random ones.

The European Space Agency's GAIA mission will create a detailed 3D chart of the galaxy by studying a small percentage of the 100 billion stars within it, with the ultimate goal of producing a map to an unparalleled degree of accuracy. This article will examine the mission itself, along with the resulting data releases and their potential impact. A detailed overview of the DR1 and DR2 data releases and their initial findings, including DR1 as a precursor to the eagerly anticipated DR2, will also be presented.

For graphs with a given number of vertices and treewidth of order $O(n^{1/2-\epsilon})$, we've devised a word-RAM algorithm that computes an $O(1)$-approximation of treewidth in $O(n)$ time, achieving better efficiency than treewidth-based algorithms when memory is a limiting factor. Furthermore, we've developed a method to obtain $k$-approximate vertex separators in $O(k^n)$ time, significantly reducing memory usage from $n$ to $k/n$.

A substantial portion of network information comes from edge weights and their directionality.
Most network measures were initially developed for simple undirected networks.
As a result, weighted network extensions were created to incorporate weight-based information, particularly for calculating the local clustering coefficient.
We discovered that not all these extensions are suitable for weighted networks and some hybrid between weighted and classical clustering that are difficult to interpret due to mixed criteria.
We therefore suggest a fully weighted definition for clustering that builds upon a well-known method and uses only weight-based network information.
We demonstrated the efficacy of this proposal using artificial and real-world networks.
Specifically, we analyzed artificial networks to showcase its advantages and a network of publications to reveal new insights.

One notable strategy to embed prior knowledge about physical systems into machine learning models is physics-informed neural networks (PINNs). These models have been observed to perform well with smaller training datasets, excel in generalizing outcomes, and reduce training time. This paper demonstrates the advantages of using PINNs compared to purely data-driven neural networks in terms of training performance. Additionally, PINNs are shown to effectively detect anomalies in real-world data, outshining purely data-driven networks in this task.

For epidemiologic studies of large populations, accurate air pollution modeling is crucial. Recent advances in exposure modeling through the integration of Geographic Information Systems and machine learning techniques offer promising opportunities to refine existing air pollution models. This research explores the potential of machine learning algorithms to improve upon a proxy model, particularly in contexts where direct exposure measurements are lacking. By modeling fine particulate matter (PM2.5) in a 17x17 km^2 area of Salt Lake City, Utah, investigators found grounds for optimism that PM2.5 levels can be accurately predicted via surface measurements, even in the absence of local emissions data. With even a small set of key variables, machine learning algorithms produced results comparable to a widely-used statistical model, although biases did exist in the estimates. This study highlights the importance of validation and quantification of model uncertainties in the application of machine learning algorithms for exposure modeling.

To differentiate between zero-energy peaks originating from Majorana and those from other causes at non-zero temperatures, our method involves swapping the normal lead in tunneling spectroscopy with a high-resistance lead (characterized by large Ohm values). The increased resistance in this setup significantly alters tunneling conductance, impacting it in distinct ways. While the Majorana peak persists in rising as temperatures decrease in proportion to T^(2r-1), any non-Majorana caused zero-energy peak follows temperature behaviors inherent to standard tunneling spectroscopy, characterized by T^(2r-1) or T^-1 laws. Additionally, for tunneling into a tripartite system where two legs are highly resistive and only one allows current flow, specific low-tunneling-strength asymptotes emerge that unambiguously identify Majorana modes.

We've developed a new method for analyzing the performance of linear bandit algorithms, 
even in complex scenarios where action spaces vary freely. By focusing on the eigenspectrum 
of the design matrix, we've established a regression-based model that determines regret 
bounds, unaffected by the actions' correlations. The approach yields sharper regret 
predictions for algorithms like SOA and Kawahara, especially in cases where features are sparse. 
To demonstrate its versatility, we've applied this method to two challenging scenarios: 
the stochastic linear MAB problem with unbalanced actions and the Gaussian process optimization 
problem, where the expected regret decreases at a rate controlled by the matrix's condition number.

Graphene with gaps has been proposed to showcase the family of non-Fermi liquid symmetries, known as emergent SO(N) symmetries, resulting in various fractional quantum Hall effects, where N is equal to 2, 3, 4, or 6. In this research, a more intense form of the orbital Hall effect is observed in a type of gapped graphene with SO(8) symmetry. A newly identified physical quantity, the orbital Chern number, solidly characterized as being a well-defined, half-integer, and parity-even property, is found to be governed by the orbital wave function's symmetry properties. In the case of a type of twisted gapped graphene, called STG8, this new quantity is found to be 4, while in the case of another type, called TG6 mut, it is found to be 3. A visually represented model illustrating the wave functions' symmetry properties was created to aid in understanding the orbital Hall effect in these materials.

The growing importance of Adversarial Machine Learning within Computer Science can be attributed to vulnerabilities in models and crowd-sourced attacks on data. Over the past two years, research has gained momentum in graph adversarial attacks but Graph Classification remains an understudied area. The indirect utilization of Reinforcement Learning methods for graph classification, given that datasets involve discrete graphs with labels, stands in contrast to traditional approaches that use direct gradient optimization. This work aims to explore the novel threat of data manipulation during training (Data Poisoning) targeting Graph Classification neural networks via Reinforcement Learning agents.

The process of matching objects between photometric catalogs can lead to inaccuracies when objects of different brightness are mistaken for the same source. However, incorporating the magnitudes of sources in the object-matching process can rectify this issue, as it allows for consideration of an object's brightness when assessing a match. We have developed a novel probabilistic framework that addresses cross-matching among multiple photometric catalogs, taking into account the selection biases that arise from using magnitude-limited catalogs. This framework not only accounts for astrophysical source properties but also simulates the biases introduced by observation techniques, resulting in a more accurate assessment of source association. We have tested the framework's effectiveness using several methods to assess its correctness. These tests involved evaluating the distribution of cluster members, the distribution of luminosity for cluster members, and the distribution of luminosity for members of background galaxies using a measure called cumulative accuracy. These tests demonstrated that the framework is effective in providing cross-matching solutions of high accuracy. Furthermore, the framework's ability to incorporate additional information from cluster mass estimates allows for the production of a comprehensive source catalog that accounts for potential members, false members, and field sources. This cluster catalog is particularly valuable, as it facilitates easy identification of false cluster members, ultimately enabling researchers to determine cluster membership through a straightforward metric.

In this paper, a hypergraph is considered as the correct framework for defining minimum hypergraph cover and maximum hypergraph independence. Specifically, a minimal vertex cover is one that uses the fewest vertices required to cover all the hyperedges, and a maximal independence is the largest set of vertices from which the hyperedges can be completely removed. Comparing this to the hypergraph's independence and cover representations in terms of size difference reveals an interesting problem: must the difference always be even? The question has been investigated and resolved with positive results under certain conditions; however, an alternative, simpler solution exists that provides an even more general outcome.

In the context of biology and medicine, knowledge ontologies play a vital role in ensuring consistency and facilitating knowledge sharing. This process involves the standardization of knowledge domains through controlled vocabulary, enabling researchers to efficiently compare and combine various datasets. Despite being essential, the adoption of knowledge ontologies among researchers and clinicians remains low. This article focuses on the role of ontologies in translational cancer research and presents three key challenges associated with incorporating ontologies into research and clinical activities. These challenges include the complexity of knowledge required to address specific research and clinical tasks, the lack of domain-specific data, and the requirement of domain experts to effectively utilize ontologies.

We introduce an innovative technique that synergistically combines inter-domain loss and CycleGAN to facilitate semi-supervised end-to-end automatic speech recognition. Inter-domain loss aims to derive a common speech-text representation through a shared neural network, whereas CycleGAN leverages cycle-consistency and identity mapping to preserve input characteristics after cross-domain conversion. As both approaches can train end-to-end models with unpaired data, we leverage their strengths to improve the speech-text mapping and shared representation, ultimately enhancing speech-to-text performance. Our experimental findings on the WSJ, Voxforge, and LibriSpeech datasets reveal significant reductions in character error rate (approximately 8-8.5%), surpassing the baseline performance and exhibiting noticeable improvements on LibriSpeech test_clean.

A fundamental theory known as active inference underpins how living beings interact with their surroundings. This theory views the brain as an efficient tool that employs Bayesian principles to create a detailed mental framework, aiming to minimize uncertainty about the world. Despite the theory's significance in cognitive neuroscience, its practical application is restricted to simplified simulations due to limitations in dealing with large and varied environments. This research incorporates the latest advancements in deep learning to create a more sophisticated mental framework, one that can be built directly from high-dimensional data, such as video feeds, without the need for pre-defined parameters. Furthermore, this work demonstrates that such frameworks can be utilized to facilitate active inference. This study marks the first instance of applying active inference using deep learning techniques to a real-world navigation task involving a robotic system.

Our study of binary mixtures used molecular dynamics simulations. The mixtures consisted of molecules made of up to four "beads" per molecule in different configurations. We explored the separation of components caused by temperature variations through the Soret effect. Our experiments revealed the opposite effect in systems with molecules composed of more than three "beads", where the MD simulations matched historic data. The behavior of the simulated systems was also compared to a mathematical model that considered the entropic and energetic contributions to the separation of components. The MD simulations showed a good match with the predicted patterns of separation. However, the actual behavior of the simulated systems differed slightly due to the specific interaction between the beads. Our study demonstrated that atomic structure affects the separation of components caused by temperature variations.

The development of Automated Essay Scoring involves a fusion of expertise from Education, Linguistics, and Natural Language Processing. Effective evaluation by an NLP model depends on its ability to identify patterns in written content, even in cases where the writing quality is subpar. Despite the current prominence of large transformer-based models in various NLP applications, these models' computational complexity poses significant practical challenges. This paper presents a new benchmark for Automated Essay Scoring, incorporating raw essay data along with accurate human ratings from the Great Barrier Reef essay dataset. We introduce a set of evaluation tasks featuring increasingly demanding goals, progressing from predicting a rough rating to assigning a more precise score and finally, inferring a human writer's level of competence. When testing on this benchmark, we discovered several popular large transformer-based models and a state-of-the-art AEs score predictor fail to generalize well to unseen data. We explored and demonstrated the significance of using NLP task-specific architectures and training environments to improve performance. The proposed benchmark is publicly available on the HuggingFace Datasets platform.

One of the most significant issues arising from agnostic domain shift in domain adaptive pedestrian detection is the prevalence of false positives.  As labeling each target domain's boxes is impractical, researchers focus on finding a solution that compensates for the shift.  To address this challenge, we introduce the Focus Loss (FL) to enhance simulated target domain training sets.  FL, a combination of classification and regression loss, prevents overfitting to simulated pseudo-positive boxes by eliminating excessive counting of false positive boxes.  If a ground truth box exists in an image, the loss function focuses on reducing the detection output's overall location bias.  To further tackle the simulated pseudo-negative class imbalance issue, we introduce Positive Patch Minus Background Loss (PPMB Loss), a more effective solution than traditional two-class loss for training with randomly cropped image patches.  PPMB Loss reduces patch-based bias by eliminating a zero-filling bias during patch-based training.  To our knowledge, this is the first adaptive loss studied in domain adaptive pedestrian detection.  Our research utilizes this setup to achieve significant gains of 5.8% and 6.3% from the state-of-the-art of 65.3% and 64.5% on the benchmark UniTime18-benchmark and the benchmark UniTime18-benchmark of 59.3 and 58.3 respectively.

This study presents an innovative technique for enhancing low-quality music recordings made by mobile devices by drawing inspiration from expertly recorded music. The analysis reveals typical flaws in low-quality recordings such as limited frequency range and added noise. To address these issues, a novel two-step method is introduced, comprising a sound representation transformation and noise removal. The representation phase involves translating the music into a format that mimics the structure of professionally recorded music. The correction phase is designed to fix the typical distortions in low-quality recordings. The technique was experimentally validated to measure its effectiveness in improving low-quality recordings.

Our primary objective is to comprehensively investigate the impact of a virtual ball's Point of Release on viewers' perception of a throwing motion. Our perceptual study revealed that individuals tend to more readily notice errors in underarm throws where the point of release occurs early, in contrast to late releases. Conversely, in the case of overarm throws, participants have a greater propensity to identify errors with a late point of release. Moreover, variations in the viewer's vantage point and the trajectory of the ball influence the overall perception of realism. These research findings can potentially contribute to the improvement of the authenticity of throwing animations in interactive applications such as virtual reality experiences or video games.

To incorporate syntax-aware decoding into Neural Machine Translation systems, a novel NMT architecture called Seq2DRNN was designed, which leverages a tree-structured DRNN (Doubly-Recurrent Neural Networks) model originally proposed in 2017 by Alvarez-Melis and Jaakola. The proposed Seq2DRNN architecture inherits the syntax-aware properties of the original model but simplifies it by integrating a syntax generator that produces root-dependent right-branching tree structures via a parameterized rule. An asynchronous Seq2DRNN architecture was further developed to integrate tree-based parsing (root-dependent or in-order) with sequence-based parsing, yielding better translations and more efficient decoding by allowing the syntax and semantics to concurrently evolve. Experiments were conducted on English and German translations with the Seq2DRNN architecture, showing a notable 2.14 BLEU-point improvement over the baseline system. An open-source implementation of the proposed architecture is made available on GitHub.

The credibility of astrochemical simulations heavily rely on the accuracy of binding energy values that take into account the diverse physical interactions present in astrophysical settings. Developing a comprehensive database of binding energy that accounts for the numerous observed species in space is an essential step in enhancing the reliability of astrochemical simulations. We initiated this process by expanding the database of binding energy, which was previously established for small molecular clusters, to now include species such as NH3, H2O, CO, and CH4, in combination with other molecules like CO2, N2, and CH3OH. A total of 62 distinct systems were examined in this study, all of which consisted of up to six molecular components, and the observed trends in binding energy are compared to theoretical predictions. A discussion on the observed trends and potential shortcomings of current theoretical models is then presented. A comprehensive database of binding energy will serve as a valuable resource for informing the development of future theoretical models as well as for refining the accuracy of astrochemical simulations in the study of comets and protoplanetary disks.

A multiplicative stochastic process with lognormally distributed lower bounds is studied, where a theoretical model of the process is developed and its distribution, characterized by four parameters, along with its statistical properties, is analytically determined. This model is further validated by demonstrating its compatibility with real-world data through parameter adjustment.

We offer novel approaches to acquire in-depth knowledge about a mysterious quantum state using an efficiently manageable number of copies. Our key contribution is a depth-controlled randomized measurement strategy that combines the capabilities of random Pauli measurements and random Clifford measurements. These can be applied using just near-term devices. Additionally, we developed a depth-controlled randomized measurement that utilizes any unitary decomposition. Our techniques are motivated by and closely related to the principles of quantum capacity and beneficial quantum channels. Our results are demonstrated through multiple applications, utilizing either random Pauli measurements or a mix of both and the more powerful random Clifford measurements.

The researchers in a particular study extended the solutions found in complex geometric optics to a related system of equations, which was initially investigated in contexts of electrical impedance tomography and the integrable Davey-Stewartson II equations, focusing particularly on the large spectral parameter $k$ in a specified reference \cite{KlSjSt20}. They now examined how this work can be applied to the reflection coefficient and derived new asymptotic formulas for specific domains with potential functions and smooth, strictly convex boundaries.

The vast majority of NLP text transformations have inherent limitations in their ability to expand coverage of input data due to the need to preserve the original class label. In order to overcome this constraint, we propose a concept called sibylvariance, which refers to the use of data transforms that can vary class labels, allowing for the creation of more diverse and comprehensive datasets. To implement this concept, we introduce two new data transformation techniques, namely the addition of an optional sentence that can be null and the duplication of sentences, both of which are designed to facilitate the creation of sibylvariant data transforms. Through comprehensive testing using SNLI and SciTail datasets, our approach has consistently outperformed standard data transformation techniques, achieving higher average accuracy for duplicate and combined transforms (0.8142 vs. 0.7895) and combined transforms (0.8205 vs. 0.7895).

Researchers aim to create meta-learning algorithms that capitalize on previous experience to rapidly acquire new skills or adapt to new environments by employing representation learning. A successful example is Model-Agnostic Meta-Learning (MAML), which leverages an optimized representation to enhance the performance of a variety of tasks. In this paper, a new meta-learning algorithm is introduced that uses reinforcement learning to determine the best feature subset for each task. In contrast to traditional meta-learning algorithms, the proposed method learns a client-specific representation by identifying the most useful features for specific tasks, rather than generalizing to all tasks. Experimental results indicate that the proposed algorithm outperforms MAML and other baseline methods in learning a consistent representation, and achieves better overall performance on a range of benchmark datasets.

Utilizing multilingual learning in state-of-the-art machine translation models can aid in adapting to low-resource languages, albeit these models are computationally costly. Knowledge distillation presents itself as a viable method to obtain a highly accurate, lightweight translation model using a resource-intensive baseline model. This study focuses on improving current distillation techniques for neural machine translation by implementing two new methods: incorporating extra contrastive loss to enhance the distilled model's capabilities. We also explore the application of knowledge distillation to sequence-to-event and natural language to SQL translation tasks, as well as examining additional distillation objectives for improving event and semantic parsing.

The Turan number for an r-uniform graph F, denoted by ex(n, F), is defined as the maximum number of edges in an F-free r-uniform graph on n vertices. The Turan density of F, denoted by pi(F), is defined as the limit of the maximum number of edges over the total possible number of edges as the number of vertices approaches infinity. Erdos-Simonovits-Sos' theorem enables the determination of Erdos-Stone-Simonovits constants for specific r = 2 graphs.
